I have heard that in the transformation and penetration of cosmic phenomena, nothing surpasses yin and yang;
in the molding and covering of all things, nothing surpasses heaven and earth.
Now, considering that the five phases had not yet taken form and there were originally no people or things, the *Yi Gouming jue* states:
"Before heaven and earth were divided,
there was the Grand Ease (*Taiyi*)."
There was the Grand Beginning (Taichu), there was the Grand Commencement (Taishi),
there was the Grand Purity (Taisu),
and there was the Grand Ultimate (Taiji).
This constitutes the five movements.
When the forms of the qi and phenomena have not yet manifested, it is called Taiyi (the Great Purity).
When the primal qi has just begun to sprout, it is called Taichu (the Great Beginning).
The initial stage of qi and form is called the Grand Beginning (Taishi).
When form undergoes transformation and possesses substance, it is called the Grand Primal (Taisu).
When substance and form are fully established, it is called the Grand Ultimate (Taiji).
Because they transform the five qi, they are called the "five movements" (wuyun).
It is said that when the qi, form, and substance are fully present yet not yet separated from one another,
these are all names for the state of "Great Ease" (Taiyi) in its fivefold manifestation.
At that time, all was empty and void;
there were as yet no people or things. Once the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) were established, their relative ranks were then defined. The *Qianzao du* states:
"The Great Ultimate (*taiji*), the Great Purity (*taisù*), and the Great One (*tài yī*)—though their names differ, their underlying principle is one."
The *Yiwei Tonggua* states:
"The Great Ultimate gives birth to the Two Polarities.
This means that the qi which is clear and light ascends to become Heaven.
That which is turbid and heavy sinks below to become the earth.
When humans are added to these, they are called the Three Powers (Sancai).
The *Yi Zhengzi* says:
Once heaven, earth, and the myriad things exist,
the positions of ruler and subject are established,

and the rites of father and son, elder and younger, husband and wife, as well as the distinctions between the honorable and the lowly, the superior and the subordinate, are fixed; thus the transformation of natural order has already arisen.
The wind of non-action spreads widely; the *Hetu Kuodi Xiang* says:
"When heaven and earth were first established, there was the Lord of Heaven (Tianhuang)."
Serene and spontaneous, he is identical to the Ultimate Dao.
He wears nine wings upon his body and rules by the virtue of Wood.
Without any deliberate action, he was transformed spontaneously.
The *Kaishan tu* states:
"Dihuang arose on Mount Xionger and Longmen."
Regarding the Fire-Virtue King,
the *Mingli xu* states:
"Renhuang rode upon six feathered creatures."
Riding a cloud-chariot, he emerged from the valley mouth;
he divided the nine provinces and governed all under heaven.
He had nine brothers.
Based on the topography of its mountains, rivers, and terrain, the land was divided into nine regions,
each occupying a single province.
The Imperial Genealogy states:
The Heavenly Sovereigns each ruled for eighteen thousand years.
Altogether, the Earthly Sovereigns governed the world for one hundred and fifty generations,
totaling fifty-four thousand years.
Next were the five lords of the Long clan: Huang Bo, Huang Zhong, Huang Shu, Huang Ji, and Huang Shao.
These five brothers all rode dragons as they ascended and descended.
In total, these one hundred and eighty reigns governed the world for nine million two hundred twenty-seven thousand three hundred and sixty years;
these were none other than the five deities, beginning with Lingwei-yang.
Next came the Lord of Shen-nong.
He rode upon six dragons and measured across the four seas; he equalized cold and heat for the people and regulated the winds and rains.
Altogether there were ten generations, each governing for nine hundred years.
Next, there are four surnames;
next, there are those who do not complete a single lifetime; next, there are seventy-two surnames;
and next, there are three surnames.
Some rode flying rams or flying deer;
they first taught the people to dwell in caves and to eat the flesh of birds and beasts.
They wore garments of skins and fur.
Next came the Lord of the Nest (Cao Shi), who rode upon dragons and麒麟 (qílín) and mounted phoenixes and tigers;
he constructed nests from wood and taught the people to dwell within them.
This was done to avoid the harm of birds and beasts.
Next came Suirenshi, who taught the people to drill wood for fire, thereby transforming raw food into cooked.
To avoid the stench of raw meat and similar things,
he cast metal blades, and the people were greatly pleased.
This constitutes six *ji* and ninety-three generations in total.
One thousand two hundred and eighty-nine generations, totaling one million ten thousand one thousand eight hundred and forty years.
From the descent from heaven, these are collectively called the Three Sovereigns (*Sanhuang*). Next were the sages with serpent bodies and ox heads; as the *Six Arts Treatise* (*Liujing lun*) states:
The Emperor Taohao, surnamed Baoxi, had the clan name Feng.
He had the body of a serpent and the head of a human,
and possessed sagely virtue.
After Suiren passed away, Fuxi the Sovereign was born.
During his era, there were fifty-nine clans.
Fuxi the Sovereign was the first to establish the order of governance.
He established ritual codes;
all were ruled by the virtue of Wood.
He instituted the rites of marriage.
He received the Dragon Chart and established his offices based on the dragon; therefore,
they were called the Dragon Masters.
He reigned for a total of eleven thousand one hundred and twelve years.
Yan Di Shennong’s surname was Jiang;
he had a human body with the head of an ox.
There was an auspicious sign of fire;
thus, he was the King of Fire Virtue (Huode Wang).

His seven generations together spanned five hundred years. Regarding the Emperor whose forehead was as level as a pearl and whose brow was like the sun, the *Lunliu* (Treatise on the Six Arts) states: [text follows].
The Sovereign of the Wagon (Xuánhuáng) was surnamed Gōngsūn; he was born at twenty-five months of age.
He possessed the marks of the pearl-forehead and the sun-cornered brow, and he ruled over the world by the virtue of Earth.
The month of Yin was established as the beginning of the year.
Twenty-five sons were born,
belonging to twelve clans.
In all, there were thirteen generations,
who together ruled for one thousand seven hundred and twenty-two years.
He received the Imperial Mandate in a dream.
He then traveled with Tian Lao along the Yellow River to receive [the teachings];
there he obtained the "River Charts and Book" from a young horse-herder boy and paid his respects to the Elder Guangcheng on Mount Kongtong.

The *Shiji of Emperors* states that the era of the Three Sovereigns lasted a total of twenty thousand and ninety-seven years; it was during this time that the eight trigrams were first drawn and the eight pure lines were doubled. The *Hetu Kuadixiang* says: "Fuxi gazed upward at the patterns of Heaven."
Observing downward, he took the earth as his model;
he first drew the eight trigrams in order to communicate with the virtue of the spiritual intelligences.
Shennong took the eight trigrams and multiplied them to form sixty-four. He established the Cloud Officials and arranged the Bird Records. The *Lun on the Six Arts* states:
"The Yellow Emperor received the auspicious omen of the Brilliant Clouds."
He used clouds to record his officials.
Because Emperor Shaohao received the auspicious omen of the phoenix, he named his offices after birds;
he taught hunting and fishing to sustain the common people.
He fashioned the plow and the hoe to provide for the people.
The *Lunyu* (Analects), in the "Discourse on the Six Arts," states: "Fuxi created nets and traps for hunting and fishing, and took sacrificial animals to fill the kitchen."
Therefore it is said: Fuxi [was the first].
Shennong cut wood to make plowshares and bent wood to make plowshafts, beginning the instruction of all under heaven to plant the five grains.
Therefore, he was titled the Lord of Divine Agriculture (Shennong). He established markets, which were founded by Shennong; he cast vessels, domesticated oxen for riding, and utilized horses.
He constructed palatial chambers, draped robes and garments, fashioned pestles and mortars, and provided boats and oars.
He modeled the tracks of birds to create writing;
he refined the rites and music through the transformation of customs—both of these occurred during the time of the Yellow Emperor.
The *Treatise on the Six Arts* states:
The Yellow Emperor had seven assistants.
Cang Jie created written characters;
Da Nao created the cycle of the sexagenary calendar.
Lishou created arithmetic;
Rongcheng created the calendar; Qibo created medical prescriptions;
Guishenqu created divination for seasonal omens.
Xi Zhong fashioned the chariot and created the pitch-pipes;

he established the rites of the sacrificial mounds and altars. This continued through to the sovereigns who aided virtue and transmitted sagehood, and the emperors whose benevolence flourished and whose sagacity was enlightened.

He appointed the offices of the Eight Xuan and Eight Kai; when Shun assumed the regency, he appointed eight men each from the lineages of Gao Yang and Gao Xin as men of talent to hold the duties of governing and tending the people.
He also commissioned Xi and He, the officials of the Eastern and Southern Tracts, belonging to the Xi and He clans.

As the official who managed the sun, moon, and the four seasons for Yao, [Shun] cultivated the hundred grains to diligently promote agriculture; Hou Ji sowed the hundred grains and disseminated the five teachings to regulate all things.
Truly reverent and capable of yielding, the myriad undertakings were all made to flourish.
He brought harmony to the myriad states and regulated the hundred clans.
He banished the four villains to the four frontiers and exiled the Sanmiao to Sanwei— Hundun, Taowu, Qiongqi, and Taotie.
Regarding the four wicked men:
Yao banished them to the four frontiers of the realm.
Then the Lord of Miao rebelled.

When Shun banished [the four criminals] to the mountains of Sanwei, he adjusted the pitch-pipes to harmonize the eight winds and observed the celestial sphere to align the seven administrative duties.
When Yu of Xia dredged the nine rivers, he succeeded his father in managing the floodwaters.
He pacified the great mountains and rivers of the Nine Provinces;
he received the Nine Categories of the Great Plan from the River God and obtained the principles of geomancy from the cavernous abodes.
Copper was contributed from the Nine Provinces to cast the Nine Cauldrons.
Eight households formed a neighborhood;
three neighborhoods formed a district.
The Three Enlightened Ones constitute the village. They ride upon four vehicles: for traveling on land they ride in a carriage;
for traveling on water they ride in a boat;
for traveling through mud they ride in a sled.
When traveling by mountain, he rode in a carriage; he accepted tributes according to the local products of each region, clearing the mountains and establishing offerings at the rivers.
When King Yin campaigned to punish the guilty and comfort the people, yellow fish and black birds gathered upon his altar and transformed into black jade.
He then attacked Jie.
His preferred colors were black and white.
He moved the Nine Cauldrons to Hao and established villages of one hundred households; he leveled the violent and stilled the chaos.
He untied the nets and cut his hair;
he rescued those drowning and extinguished the flames.
Thus it came to pass that in the magnificent Zhou dynasty, there were many eminent scholars gathered in great numbers.
The virtue of the *Guanju* and the "Stag’s Hoof" was such that Ji Li’s consort, Da Ren, dreamed of a great man entering her womb;
she subsequently gave birth to King Wen. King Wen’s consort, Da Si, gave birth to King Wu, Fa.
The month of Zi was established as the beginning of the year, and red was the honored color.
Five households formed a neighborhood (*lin*).
Within the royal domain, there were the administrative units of *bi*, *ju*, *zu*, *dang*, *zhou*, and *xiang*.
While the Duke of Zhou was acting as regent, criminals were apprehended;
yet in autumn there occurred a portentous transformation of thunder and wind,
which bent the grain and uprooted the trees.
He opened the book sealed with golden cinnabar,
whereupon he welcomed the Duke of Zhou back and divined for a site to settle at Luo.
He measured out the lands and established the capital;
he formulated the rites and composed the music.
He died at Feng and was buried at Bi.
The *Guanju* praises the virtue of the royal consort;

the *Linzhi* extols the lineage of benevolent men. The *Feng* of Zhounan and Shaonan signifies that the cultural transformation of Zhou and Shao spread from the north to the south. Regarding the arrangement of the five elements and six rectitudes: wood, metal, water, fire, and earth constitute the five elements.
Foreseeing future events,
promoting the good and elevating the worthy,
they were reverent and diligent, never falling into negligence.
He clearly examined the laws and statutes;
he declined emoluments and yielded honors;
when the ruler erred, he remonstrated with him.
These constitute the six administrative measures. The system of the nine fields and four *jing* (well-fields) is established: three *wu* (blocks) form one *jing*, and nine such fields are laid out.

The rites for bestowing robes and ceremonial gifts are arranged, detailing the five grades of vestments and the protocol for the nine types of regalia. The regulations for the war chariots are expanded, and the ten-fold system is extended to the city walls.
The city produced a single chariot of leather as a model for the world and a canonical authority for all things;
though distant and remote, three ages have passed since its founding,
and vast and far-reaching, a hundred kings have succeeded one another through time.
Wherever the Sage’s virtue extends and his divine transformation reaches,
the Dragon Court and Phoenix Nesters await the seasonal breath to present their treasures;
from the lands of the Sun and the Continent of Qilin, they observe the winds and come to submit at the borders.
Springs and dew manifest their rare flavors;
plants and trees transform into auspicious forms.
With the jaw of a swallow and the body of a fish.
They shine resplendent among the feathered tribes;
with wolf-like hooves and ox-like tails,
they radiate brilliance within the flocks of fur-bearing creatures.
Virtue alone moves Heaven, and auspicious omens truly gather;
thus there is the "Song of the Sovereign’s Prolonged Brilliance" and the "Song of the Limbs’ Utmost Goodness."
The Zhou divined for eternal years, and the Yin praised their many generations.
As for the Way, human relations receive its benefits and are thereby established.
All things rely upon it for their existence;
states depend upon it to avoid calamity;
and sovereigns and ministers rely upon it to achieve good governance.
His virtuous governance transformed all under heaven, its influence reaching both the Chinese and the barbarians;
his Way permeated the five regions, and his benevolence was extended to the common people.
His achievements and deeds were both grand and enduring.
The principles for the time are complete;
the utility for the world is sufficient.
As for the immortal prescriptions of Laozi, their intent lies in the transformation of the body into a feathered being.
Śākyamuni and Brahmā originally vowed to enter nirvāṇa;
they have cast their physical bodies into the Great Clarity and roam their spirits within the realm of eternal bliss.
He prizes the refinement of the physical form for the sake of immortality,
seeking quiescent illumination within the unborn.
He constructs parables of the great Peng bird and the small swallow.
Zhang Guo’s unfounded speculations are no different from Zou Yan’s discourse on the heavens, which ultimately leads only to the obscure and the vast;
Yu Qiu’s explication of dreams is but a vain display of flowery rhetoric.
Now, the Great Tang governs with supreme authority as the Sage Emperor presides with effortless ease.
He honors the worthy and honors the aged, and prizes virtue and prizes benevolence;
thus, the transformation of restoring the correct way has already spread far and wide.
The wind of returning to simplicity spreads far and wide;
in principle, one must abandon the complex for the simple and discard the false to return to the true.
I, a fool, believe that regarding the two streams of Buddhism and Daoism, they are not urgent matters of state governance.
I have long desired to present this for Your Majesty’s consideration; I venture to offer a brief discussion upon it.
Without presuming to judge my own doubts, I dare to set forth what I have yet to fully comprehend.
"Your Excellency possesses extensive knowledge of antiquity and has profoundly investigated the origins of learning.
We would be grateful for your detailed analysis of the essential points regarding what should be offered or rejected, and what is acceptable or unacceptable.
Thereupon, the eminent scholar of the Right Academy composed his countenance and sat with solemn dignity.
After a long while, he said to him,
"This is different from what I have heard.
The Discourse says:
Observing the phenomena of heaven,
one sees the divisions of the degrees and positions of the sun, moon, and five planets;
observing the phenomena of earth, one sees...
Thus one knows the place where the hundred rivers and four great streams converge;
by observing the traces of antiquity and the present,
one ascends in form to the time before the Taiji and the Primordial Chaos.
To perceive future events before they have even sprouted,
without the slightest doubt as minute as a hair or a dust mote—
this is what is called wisdom.
Since you already know this yet ask again,
I shall likewise recount it and provide a brief explanation,
examining the teachings of the Six Classics of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius.
Loyalty and filial piety constitute its foundation;
the two essays on Li Lao mark its initial sprouting.
Virtue and Way inaugurate its beginning.
The texts of the Tripiṭaka of Gautama take compassion as their foundation;
although the specific accounts differ, the underlying principles and logic are no different.
All are perfectly beautiful and perfectly good;
they are worthy of veneration and emulation.
Therefore, one discusses the myriad subtleties with a vacant mind.
He opens up skillful means to draw others in.
I have previously met Master Yuanyou and have heard much from him as well.
He spoke with comprehensive discourse,
fully recounting the Three Teachings and concurrently presenting the Nine Schools of thought.
The Master had long since withdrawn into mountain retreats, so his name and clan were unknown to all.
His deportment was serene and elegant, his every advance and retreat worthy of observation;
his speech and laughter were warm and expansive, and his movements were governed by proper measure.
Although his words contained critical evaluations, his intent remained free from praise or blame.
He subsisted on rice, cakes, pine, and yam, such that his age could not be measured;
he dwelt and slept amidst mists and clouds, thoroughly familiar with the eras of antiquity.
As for the origins and developments of the three ancient periods, they appeared as clearly as in a mirror.
The branches and offshoots of the hundred schools were as clear as the palm of one's hand;
he exhausted the sublime canons of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,
and investigated the grand regulations of Buddhism and Daoism.
Examining what they harbor within, it lies in *xīyáo* (carefree wandering) and the equalizing of all things;
observing what they esteem,
it returns to the emptiness of the nature of equality.
During a moment of leisure from his quiet seclusion,
the Master looked toward me and said,
"In this world, those who do not understand are many, and they constantly pass judgment on one another."
Thus, he affirms what is to be affirmed and negates what is not to be affirmed,
yet does not negate that which is not to be negated.
Yet they do not condemn what they themselves do not condemn;
thus, they affirm what they themselves condemn and condemn what they themselves affirm.
Now, in discussing the teachings of Confucianism,
the intent lies in managing the household so that it is orderly and the elders and juniors maintain their proper sequence;
in being free from arrogance when in superior positions and free from disorder when in subordinate ones.
Ministers and sons exhaust their loyalty and filial piety;
servants and concubines give full vent to their joyous hearts.
On a grand scale, they match Heaven in their sacrifices to the Emperor, honoring their parents and offering ancestral feasts.
I desire that Heaven and Earth may clearly observe and that the spirits and deities may manifest their numinous power,
so that calamities do not arise and disasters and chaos do not occur.
On a smaller scale, one should pursue advantage and seize the opportune moment, while being careful of oneself and practicing frugality.
He governs within the inner chambers of his household and extends his grace to those below, even to his servants;
all revere his service, and each finds what is appropriate for them.
The teaching of the Dao explains why all things come into being and how the ultimate achievement is accomplished.
It must arise from the formless and proceed from the nameless;
yet that which is formless and nameless is the source of all things.
To describe the Dao, it is both the beginning and the mother.
When discussing the teachings, there is both the mundane and the sublime.
Thus, Yuanshi remained reverently silent upon the Golden Terrace,
while the Most High draped his robes upon the Purple Palace.
He dispatched two Transcendents to guide the secular world and commanded the Five Elders to unfold the celestial charts.
Treading upon the profound, he was luminous; embracing the One, he was steadfast.
They rest in tranquility within the Great Lo and recline in the Supreme Clarity;
only then do they establish the transformation of non-action.
He practiced the teaching of non-speaking.
He disseminated the texts of the Yellow Court and the Purple Palace,
and conferred the registers of the Golden Tablet and Silver Cord.
The subtlety of dark frost and crimson snow;
the wonder of jade-essence and cloud-refinement;
the splendor of the nine-clouds bright mirror.
The brilliance of the eight refined divine elixirs is sufficient to restore youth and repel aging;
it is sufficient for one to mount feathered carriages and attain eternal life.
Wandering through the Garden of Langyuan, one forgets to return;
bathing in the Xianchi Pond, one does not come back.
Suddenly, one dons coarse cloth at the Changhe Gate.
Some control cranes on Mount Penglai;
they contemplate in stillness upon the slopes of Mount Gushan;
they ponder the subtle mysteries atop Mount Kongtong.
It endures as long as heaven and earth and shares in the alternation of darkness and light with yin and yang—
such is the teaching of the Buddha.
How magnificent! It encompasses the Flower Treasury World,
emerging beyond the nine-layered celestial canopy.
It brilliantly illuminates the Cloud Terrace,
transcending the external forms of the eight directions;
it is not a color, yet it is the wondrous color.
His radiant light intermingles before the Primordial Unity;
his divided bodies and transformational forms array themselves at the inception of the Great Void.
Therefore, through its vast and pervasive nature, it gives rise to yin and yang;
by means of its crucible and hammer, it completes heaven and earth—
the image of the Great Image.
Nurturing all within the four phenomena,
it is the material of the firm substance;
it circulates through the five elements.
The Jade Balance turns far beyond sight;
its mechanism is unfathomable.
The joined orbs hang suspended in vast infinity.
Thoroughly examining its transformation, it is neither bright nor obscure; it is subtle yet manifest.
It unifies the spiritual treasury of all the sages.
He attends the auspicious assembly of all living beings;
thus, he emerges from the burning house and provides the three vehicles,
enters the river of craving and wields the eight oars, manifesting this rare and marvelous event.
How could it be that the inconceivable is taught only in the Āmra Park,
or that it occurs only in the kingdom of Magadha?
Through various skillful means and individual acts of compassion,
they break the cage of birth and death and ferry beings to the other shore of nirvana.
There were none whose minds did not flash with the brilliance of the wish-fulfilling jewel and whose wisdom-torches did not radiate concentrated luster;
they gathered the waters of a hundred rivers,
deepening the Eastern Sea upon the earth.
It serves as the guiding thread for the myriad phenomena,
dwelling above the North Pole like Heaven;
how could it possibly be swayed by relative heights and depths, or be entangled in the rivalries between Confucianism and Mohism?

as for the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi),
both the provisional and the ultimate are thereby extinguished.

seeking the essence of their skillful and harmonious resonance.
The merit of his molding and bearing of the burden is beyond comparison with the work of creation;
daily life cannot even begin to emulate it.
This is sufficient to encapsulate the four great elements and transcend the three luminous realms in an instant.

The young master said:
It is indeed beautiful,
yet it remains suspicious;
for there is nothing that can rectify the state like the possession of loyalty.
In nourishing one's closest kin, nothing surpasses the practice of filial piety.
In traversing heaven and earth, nothing surpasses the cultivation of civil culture.
In settling calamity and disorder, nothing surpasses the discourse on military affairs.
In stabilizing those above and below, nothing surpasses the promotion of ritual propriety (*li*).
In transforming customs and habits, nothing surpasses the practice of music (*yue*).
This is truly the essential instruction for sovereigns and kings.
It is also the great method for cultivating the Way.
It contains the compassionate discourse of Vimalakīrti and the profound treatises on morality and virtue bequeathed by the Sage of Li.
It does not yet address the urgent needs of saving the world;
it remains like the words concerning the "wooden bird and the wild goose.
It is not only that I have not yet become your guest.
Furthermore, regarding the shared departure of the worthy, a man of broad understanding said:
"Slow speech and quick action are what the gentleman praises;
do not take your own meager learning as a standard for judging the *Dianlun*."
Have you not heard the admonition of the Marquis of Lu?
"Do not speak much; do not act much.
To speak much is to bring much harm."
There are many affairs and many troubles.
If one serves parents or sacrifices oneself for a lord, then loyalty and filial piety are the primary concerns.
If one seeks to distance oneself from harm and preserve the integrity of the person, then the Way and its Virtue (Dao-de) are the starting point.
To benefit sentient beings and rescue them from suffering, one takes compassion as the fundamental source;
to serve with filial piety and cherish loyalty, one can bring peace to the entire family and state;
and by practicing the Way and establishing virtue, one can spread one’s reputation throughout the world.
By giving rise to compassion and mobilizing pity, one can rescue the multitudes of beings.
To rescue the multitudes is to extend equal grace to the six realms of existence;
whereas to disseminate one's physical presence and reputation merely brings glory to cover a single family.
The entire family, state, and nation thus encompass the achievement of unifying the nine provinces.
Therefore, loyalty and filial piety serve as the teachings for instructing the customs of society,
while morality and virtue serve as the arts for maintaining the self.
The practice of compassion covers and nurtures all things;
it is like the heavens having three luminaries or a tripod having three legs—
each is named for its virtue and manifests its merit accordingly.
If one follows and reveres them,
one may bring about auspicious blessings.
The young master said:
The *Bibliographic Treatise* (*Yiwenzhi*) of the Former Han states:
"There are nine schools in total for preserving the person and protecting the state.
The first is called the Confucian school (*ruliú*)."
This means that he followed the principles of Yin and Yang to set forth his teachings;
he recounted the governance of the ages of Tang and Yu,
and took the Way of Confucius as his primary model.
The second is called the "Stream of the Way" (Dàoliú).
This refers to those who maintain weakness and humility,
extolling the virtue of Yao and Shun’s yielding of the throne through ritual courtesy.
It clarifies the art of governing while facing south.
It upholds the "humble and humble" (*qianqian*) of the *Yi*.
Third is the "Flow of Yin and Yang."
This refers to following the celestial calendar and its astronomical phenomena to reverently bestow the seasons upon the people.
The fourth is called the Flow of Law (*dharmasrotas*);
this refers to clarifying rewards and enacting laws to assist the ritual system.
The fifth is called the School of Names (Mingliu),
which refers to the correct enumeration of positions and names such that speech accords with the accomplishment of affairs.
The sixth is called the School of Mo (Moliu).
This refers to the ancestral sacrifices in the pure temple, the nourishing of the aged, and the bestowing of benefits.

The seventh is called the "Flowing of the Vertical and Horizontal," which refers to receiving a mandate to serve as an envoy, responding with specialized diplomacy, and exercising discretion in affairs.
The eighth is the miscellaneous stream (*miśravāda*).
This refers to that which combines the standards of Confucianism and Mohism, and encompasses the teachings of the School of Names (*Mingjia*) and Legalism (*Falun*).
He understands the fundamental principles of statecraft, such that no matter is not encompassed.
Ninth is the "Flow of Agriculture," which means encouraging plowing and sericulture and providing a comprehensive account of food and wealth.
By following its Way, one can bring peace to all things;
by practicing its affairs, one can benefit the state.
Thus, the governance of government is complete.
This is sufficient for the people.

one who is skilled at binding uses no rope or tether. "Eliminate the excessive" and "eliminate the extravagant": here, "the excessive" refers to gluttony and lust for sound and color;

it means that these three things must be abandoned. When one acts with centrality and harmony through non-action (wuwei), [the mind becomes tranquil].
Then the world will transform itself spontaneously. Be decisive, yet do not be boastful; be decisive, yet do not be self-aggrandizing.
Be decisive, yet do not be arrogant; be decisive, yet do not be overbearing.
Examine the reasons for this.
However, while suppressing worldly passions has recently served as a lesson for the age,

When we examine the time of the Yellow Emperor:

He was the crown of the Confucian scholars.

for they understood the pivot of speech.
The subtlety of this knowledge may serve as an indelible admonition for the kings of a hundred generations;
yet the Bodhisattva has instead treated it as a worldly instruction, equating it with secular classics.
"If that is so," the Bodhisattva said,
"those of great wisdom linger amidst mountains standing like pillars."
Those of small capacity are like tumbleweeds blown by the wind or duckweed floating on the surface.
I have heard that when one acts upon what can be done during a time when it can be done,

I now show this to you so that you may understand what can be done and what can be avoided.
Indeed, the five colors lead to blindness;
this means that greed for and attachment to beautiful forms injure the vital essence and result in loss of sight.
Is this not what the Vimalakīrti Sūtra means when it says that the forms one perceives are like those seen by the blind?
The five sounds lead to deafness;
that is to say, indulging in licentious sounds damages the harmony of the mind.
One cannot hear the music of silence.
Is this not what Vimalakīrti meant when he said that all sounds heard are equal to echoes?
Even the five flavors can cause a sense of refreshment.
This means that when a person indulges in the five flavors, the sense of taste is impaired and one becomes weary of life.

By not valuing rare treasures, one puts an end to theft.
Is this not observing that sensation is impermanent?
Not seeing what is desirable leads to stillness;
is this not stillness?
Is it not by contemplating the impurity of the body?
By removing distraction one causes the mind to become empty;
by cherishing the essence and blood, one causes the bones to become strong.
Thus, there is a mind that can be made empty and bones that can be made firm.
When the vital breath disperses and the form withers, it is not because the mind was not empty;
when the spirit departs and the body decays, it is not because the bones were not firm.
"To blunt their sharpness" means to eliminate discursive thought;

This simply means to suppress their cleverness and bring their contentious struggles to rest.
To maintain purity and frugality while avoiding conflict with others is merely the singular resolve of a scholar;
it is not the great magnanimity of a man of comprehensive vision.
He harmonizes with the light so as not to disturb others;
he blends with the dust so as not to distinguish himself.
He does this simply to wash away the waves and stir up the mud in order to avoid calamity.
To be unable to benefit others through communal practice (*samānārthatā*) in order to transform sentient beings constitutes conditioned activity and a concern for things;
it is not unconditioned and free from affairs.
To seek harmony by means of oneself while remaining ignorant of how things harmonize of their own accord is likewise so.

It stumbles within the confines of physical form and is entangled within the realm of conceptual discrimination.
The example makes this clear.

The Way flows forth from the methods of the immortals;
the Buddha fundamentally resides in the teachings of the divine.

This is why one returns the years, reverses aging, prolongs the blossoms, and sustains the radiance.

As for the Buddha, he necessarily renounces kin and spouse, makes his body and nature leisurely, takes pure awakening as his teacher, and trusts in conditions and destiny; by returning to the One and transcending birth, he is able to accomplish the holy enterprise.
Their wisdom transcends the Great Illumination, and their resolve encompasses kalpas as vast as the Ganges;

The substance of the Dao is nameless and non-active;

The Mother of the Myriad Things.
This means that the Dao does not emerge from the initial non-existence of things, but rather provides sustenance through their present existence;
thus, it is the case that what was originally non-existent now exists.
Having existed, it returns to non-existence;
thus one is constrained between existence and non-existence,
within the very source of generation and formation.
Please allow me to explain this.
According to ultimate truth, there is nothing.
Non-being is the beginning of heaven and earth.
From the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it exists.
It is the mother of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
As a mother, she is capable of giving birth.
Therefore, it is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Because it is the beginning, it is the root;
therefore, it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
According to conventional truth, things exist;
they do not exist as non-existent.
According to ultimate truth, they are non-existent.
It is not that existence becomes non-existence;
it is not that non-existence becomes existence. It is not that there is existence within existence.
It is not existent and thus non-existent;
it is not that non-existence itself is absent.
It is not non-existent and thus existent, whereby the view of eternalism naturally vanishes.
Since it does not exist, the view of nihilism ceases;
that which is "not having existence" is neither existent nor non-existent.
"Not non-existent" means that it is neither non-existent nor not non-existent.
To say that it "exists" is to say that it is not existent.
It is neither existent nor non-existent;
thus, those who cling to it lose it, and those who act upon it ruin it.
You know that difference is indeed difference.
If one does not know the reason why things differ,
nor the basis upon which they differ,
how can one know the reason why sameness and difference themselves differ?
If one does not know why differences differ from one another,
how can one know why those differences themselves differ?
If one does not know why those differences differ, [how can one know anything at all?]
How can one know the difference between identity and identity?
One does not yet know the difference between identity and identity;
how then can one know the difference between non-identity and non-difference?
If one does not know the reason why "neither identical nor different" is distinct [from other states],
how can one know the reason why "not non-identical and not non-different" is distinct?
One does not yet know the reason why "not non-identical and not non-different" is distinct.

One does not yet understand why "non-non-difference" and "non-non-distinction" differ.
How can one know difference and identity? There is no difference that does not arise from non-difference; this is the reason why difference exists.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma always relies upon the two truths, giving rise to compassion to save all beings.

The Bodhisattva’s metaphor states:

I shall now briefly recount for you the kings of ten successive dynasties, the high ministers and state counselors, and the erudite scholars of vast learning who revered and had faith in the Buddha, so as to inform you.

Emperor Wu, the Ancestor of the Jin Dynasty, possessed a majestic and extraordinary countenance; he transformed the era through his great brilliance and extensively propagated Buddhist affairs, establishing numerous monasteries. Emperor Hui of the Jin Dynasty likewise turned his heart toward the wondrous Way.
In accord with his aspiration for the profound mystery,
he subsequently established Xingsheng Temple in Luoyang to provide offerings for a hundred monks.
Emperor Min of the Jin dynasty, being deeply devoted to spiritual resonance, caused divine icons to descend from afar.
Furthermore, he established the Tongling and Baima monasteries in Chang’an; thus, during the Western Jin dynasty,
there were one hundred and eighty monasteries combined in the two capitals,
where thirteen translators produced seventy-three works of translated scripture.

There were more than three thousand seven hundred monks and nuns. During the reign of Emperor Yuan of the Jin Dynasty’s Zhongzong, when his civilizing influence extended across the land and he restored the dynasty in Jiangzuo, he constructed the two monasteries of Waguan and Longgong.
During the Jin dynasty, under Emperor Ming (Suzong), who was wise, sagacious, and possessed profound insight, he ordained a thousand monks in Danyang and Jianye.
He established vegetarian feasts to cultivate merit and constructed two monasteries, Huangxing and Daochang.

The hundred monks who had gathered to study the teachings and whose reputations were renowned— under the profound sincerity of Emperor Cheng of the Jin Dynasty’s Xianzong era, which reached a spiritual resonance with the sages and moved them through its far-reaching virtue—
constructed the two monasteries of Zhongxing and Luye.

He assembled one thousand monks who were scholars of the translated scriptures and their meanings. Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty (the later Emperor Ai) extended invitations to his attendants to discuss the subtle principles for transforming the mind; in this assembly of noble guests, he engaged in earnest dialogue and greatly manifested the "Dragon Light. Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty (the second Tai Zong) was characterized by benevolence, forbearance, gentleness, and magnanimity.
He acted with saintly reverence and clarity;

he commissioned statues, established vegetarian feasts, ordained monks, and founded monasteries. At the ancient stupa of Changgan, he erected a wooden pagoda that was magnificent and extraordinary. Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty’s Liezong era devoted his heart to the Dharma.
His aspirations and mindfulness were in profound accord with the divine. The King of the Lion Kingdom,
admiring his devotion to the Way, dispatched the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema.
He sent the jade image far away to express his sincere devotion.

He summoned monks of righteous understanding to establish Huangtai Temple and donated his former residence to become Benqi Temple. Emperor Jin’an was steadfast in his faith and never grew weary of it.
During the reign of Emperor Fuxing, the Great Shisi Temple was established to the right of the King Aśoka Stūpa in the one hundred and fourth year of the Eastern Jin dynasty;
the total number of temples combined reached one thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight.
Twenty-seven translators produced two hundred and sixty-three works.
There were twenty-four thousand monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, the Martial August, initiated his sagely reign and established the first year of the era.
Returning to purity and reverting to simplicity,
he recited the Sanskrit texts orally and transcribed the precept scriptures by hand;
he also constructed Linggen and Fawang Monasteries.

He made offerings to invite sages and worthies and studied extensively with a thousand monks. Emperor Taizong Ming of the Song dynasty, whose reign was characterized by enlightened governance and flourishing prosperity, recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* sutra daily.
He commissioned four gilded statues one zhang eight chi tall; when they could not be cast successfully, he reduced their height to one zhang four chi.
It was immediately perfected and adorned with accomplishment;
it stood eight *zhang* high.
At dawn he broke his fast, whereupon he was moved by the appearance of śarīra relics;
he then constructed Hongpuzhong Temple to invite renowned monks. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Taizu, observed the fast and abstained from killing.
With a sincere mind, he aspired to the Way.
Shangzhi’s refined discourse took the Buddha’s precepts as his fundamental principle.
That he has brought about great peace through his practice is truly in accordance with Your Majesty’s sagely intent.
Chin-yang Qunazhu (欽仰求那務) sought to promote the Great Dharma and constructed Chan-yun Temple,
where he constantly provided offerings to a thousand monks. During the Song dynasty, there were a total of one thousand nine hundred and thirteen temples.
Twenty-three translators produced two hundred and ten works;
these eminent monks and wise scholars were as dense as rice and hemp.
The jeweled lands and golden wheels stand as dense as bamboo and reeds;
the teachings of Śākyamuni flourish, and those of sincere faith are doubly numerous.
There are thirty-six thousand monks and nuns.
Emperor Taizu Gao of the Qi dynasty personally transcribed the Lotus Sūtra,
recited the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra from memory,
and regularly cast golden images on the eighth day of the fourth month.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, offerings were presented at the Pusisi temple for three hundred monks.
The Zhiqui and Zhengguan temples were established, while the Zhaoxian and Youxuan temples were built by Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty.
Three hundred monks were assembled to study the teachings and translate the scriptures.

Over the course of four years, the three traditions were compared and examined under the auspices of Emperor Gaozong Ming of the Qi dynasty, who commissioned the transcription of the entire Buddhist canon and the creation of a golden statue weighing one thousand jin.
He recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* aloud and constantly turned the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. He established monasteries for taking refuge and summoned monks to practice dhyāna.
Personally, he observed the six fast days and was dedicated to cultivating the ten wholesome deeds. During his lifetime, there were a total of two thousand and fifteen monasteries combined.
There were sixteen translators who produced seventy-two works.
There were thirty-two thousand five hundred monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu, the High Ancestor of the Liang dynasty, was of vast and magnificent character.
His discernment was clear and eminent;
his mind roamed through the seven factors of enlightenment,
and his thoughts were refined through the eight dhyānas.
He composed the *Wushi lun* (Treatise on the Five Periods) and translated works such as the *Fangdeng jing*.
He founded five monasteries, including Guangzhai and Tongtai.
At Chongyun Hall, he lectured for a multitude of a thousand monks, and throughout the realm, the six fast days were universally observed;
the myriad people all received the eight precepts. Emperor Jianwen of the Liang dynasty was naturally brilliant and lofty in character.
The Wind Deity, transcendent and surpassing, entrusted his heart to the wondrous Dharma;
having extensively studied the profound scriptures,
he established Ziji and Jibao En temples.
He pricked his own blood to transcribe ten copies of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
On the anniversary of the Empress Dowager’s death, he observed a fast and abstained from food.
He also compiled over two hundred fascicles of the *Dharmasaṃgraha-śāstra*.

The *Fǎbǎoliánbì* (Jeweled Tablets of the Dharma), comprising approximately four hundred chapters, was compiled by Emperor Xiaoyuan of the Liang dynasty’s Zhongzong. Possessing sagely versatility and penetrating spiritual insight, he established the two monasteries of Tianju and Tiangong.
He summoned a thousand monks of high reputation and noble conduct;

he himself lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and frequently expounded the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. During the Liang dynasty, there were a total of two thousand eight hundred and forty-six monasteries.
Forty-two translators translated two hundred and thirty-eight works.
There were more than eighty-two thousand seven hundred monks and nuns.
Emperors Xiao Xuan and Xiao Ming of the Liang dynasty governed with civilizing wisdom.
A great treasure for the restoration [of the state].
The altars of the later Liang dynasty brought glory to the common people.

In Jingzhou, he established the Tianhuang, Zhiqu, Daming, Baoguang, Sifang, and other monasteries. During the reigns of the two successive emperors of the Later Liang, the capital was at Jiangling for thirty-five years.
There are one hundred and eight temples.
Among the mountain temples are Qingxi, Lükxi, Fùchuán, Lóngshān, Jiǔshān, and others;
all possess solemn and magnificent Buddhist rites, with halls and buildings exquisitely carved and adorned.
Upon seeing [the Buddha], they immediately resolved their minds; upon seeing him, they forgot their return home.
There were three thousand two hundred monks and nuns.
Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty, the August Sovereign, having received the precious mandate to rule and attending the assembly of prosperity, acted as the shepherd of the people.
He was eight chi in height;
his beard was three chi long;
and fine hairs curled over his ears.
His hands hang down past his knees.
By the power of his great vows, he brings relief and salvation to all sentient beings;
by means of his great adornments, he subdues and eliminates manifold hardships.
Reflecting eternally upon the city of Pei, he desired to repay the bounty of the earth;
he wished that the capital of Qiao might likewise share in this auspicious celebration.
In the second year of the Yongding era, he established Dong'an Temple in Yangzhou.
Furthermore, for the sake of his family, the state, and all living beings,
he established four monasteries— Xinghuang, Tianju, and others— within the jurisdiction of the capital city of Yangdu.
All were adorned with embroidered checkerboard patterns, carved pillars, ornate carvings, and plastered walls.
The three tiers are solemn yet gracefully curved;
the thousand pillars shine with brilliant clarity.
Tall flagstaffs stand in rows along the broad thoroughfare.
Its lofty gates overlook the imperial carriage road;
its magnificent Vihāra is perhaps without peer, serving as a sanctuary for virtuous conduct and benevolence.
How could anything compare?
He transcribed the twelve collections of all the sutras and fashioned one million images of the Buddha's body made of gold, copper, and other materials.
He ordained seven thousand monks and nuns and restored thirty-two old temples.
Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty, the Son of Heaven, propagated and flourished the Three Jewels.
He widely propagated the Five Vehicles;
his abundant grace is comparable to the clouds of compassion,
and his great illumination is like the sun of wisdom.
His glorious reputation extends throughout the four seas;
his benevolent heart penetrates the Three Spirits.
The *diaodou* drums have no cause for alarm.
He brought his weapons to rest and repaired sixty old temples,
copying fifty sets of the entire Buddhist canon.
He ordained three thousand monks and nuns.
Emperor Xiaozhuan of the Chen dynasty held a jade tablet as he led the central command,
and he mounted the golden wheel to point toward the supreme realm.
With Dan and Shi presiding over the affairs of state on earth,
the years were bountiful and the people attained great abundance.
Within the realm there were no affairs,
and all under heaven enjoyed peace and prosperity.
He established Taihuang Temple within Jinzhong Li in Yangzhou.
Nevertheless, because his feelings regarding the solemnity of funeral rites and the honoring of distant ancestors were so earnest,
he constructed a seven-story wooden stupa at Taishang Temple for the sake of the late Consort, the Filial and Honored Tai-fei of King Shao-ling of Shixing.
The golden basin vies in brilliance with the sun,
and the pearl-encrusted wheels compete in radiance with the joined jade disks;
furthermore, it surpasses the imperial splendor of Emperor Guangwu’s abdication of the throne.
On behalf of [Emperor] Pei, he succeeded to the family legacy and established a field of merit by constructing the Chongchong (Magnificent) Imperial Monastery.
In the second year of the Taian era, he rebuilt it for the sake of the late Empress Dowager Xiaotai of King Shaozheng of Shixing.
How could he fail to reach the common people?
He erected a sacred stupa fifteen zhang high, within which he enshrined a relic of the Buddha’s fingernail.
It was two cun long and one cun wide; it was adorned and polished,
enshrined within a precious niche, and stored in various jeweled caskets.
Sometimes light flew forth in five colors and flames rose a fathom high;
his spiritual transformations were inexhaustible,
and those who beheld them were transformed at the break of dawn.
He commissioned twenty thousand statues, including those made of gold and copper;
he restored one million three hundred thousand old images;
and he transcribed the twelve scriptural collections of all the sutras.
He repaired fifty old temples and ordained ten thousand monks and nuns.
The above concerns the five sovereigns of the Chen dynasty.
In total, there were thirty-four years [of records].
There were one thousand two hundred and thirty-two monasteries,
including seventeen newly established by the state.
There are sixty-eight establishments built by the hundred officials.
Within the city walls, there are more than three hundred large temples.
According to the *Yudi tu* (Map of the Carriages and Horses): [text continues].
Originally, there were more than seven hundred temples within the capital; however,
following the outbreak of the rebellion by Hou Jing,
they were all burned to the ground and utterly destroyed.
There was the Great State of Chen;
from the high officials down to the common people, all engaged in construction.
Their gabled roofs and ridgepoles were joined together, standing as densely packed as the houses of the imperial capital.
Stūpas and monuments stand facing one another, spread out like stars beneath the capital;
the scriptures transcribed and the images fashioned are beyond reckoning.
There were also great "unrestricted" assemblies (pañcavārṣika) for the offering of alms and the support of the Saṃgha.
He practiced the release of captive creatures and the remission of punishments, widely proclaiming the ten wholesome deeds and guiding the four classes of people;
his achievements are truly difficult to match.
There were thirty-two thousand monks and nuns.
Three individuals translated eleven works of the scriptures.
These were the rulers of the Five Dynasties.
He was devoted to the profound mysteries of the sublime doctrine and extensively propagated the Buddha’s work.
He established monasteries, fashioned images, and summoned renowned monks;
during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he brought peace to the people and provided for their livelihoods.
The Emperor Zhongzong of Jin possessed the lands south of the Yangtze River;
the imperial brilliance grandly sustained the precious destiny,
and Emperor Xiaowu brilliantly inaugurated the wind of virtue.
Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty’s profound anxieties gradually began to ease, yet his progress toward the throne remained obstructed.
For two years, his path was blocked by thorns and he exhausted himself in four successive battles;
thus, a hundred concerns filled his breast.
He consolidated the myriad affairs of state within his breast;
he never grew weary of the practice of *dāna*,
and constantly maintained a mind dedicated to protecting the Dharma.
He revered and honored the Mahāyāna, gazing up with devotion at the Śrīvatsa-marked head;
he recited the scriptures from the Dragon Palace, propagating the holy teachings without weariness,
his pure voice never ceasing.
Emperor Taizu of the Song Dynasty employed these principles daily and spread them throughout the world to achieve great peace.
He constantly manifested the benevolence of releasing trapped animals from a net and yearned to return to the governance of the "knotted cords" era.
Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty penetrated the profound mysteries of truth and falsehood;
he exhausted the refined essence of Confucianism and Mohism,
cultivating the highest goodness and illuminating the flourishing era of the "Lower Wu."
Emperor Gaozu of the Liang dynasty followed in the footsteps of those of transcendent virtue and trod upon the sacred path of Vimalakīrti;
he re-knotted the cords of the earth that had already been rent asunder.
When the celestial net was collapsing,
he sought his robes even before dawn and sat waiting for the break of day;
with self-exertion and ceaseless effort, he earnestly maintained the constant patterns of human relations.
As for the profound scriptures of Vulture Peak and the esoteric meanings of the Kukkutārāma,
the principles of the two truths and five vehicles,
and the texts of the three baskets and nine divisions:
What the Red-Bearded One [Paramārtha] did not clarify,
and what the Blue-Eyed One [Kumārajīva] did not explain,
has now been fully obtained.
I do not reread the texts nor reflect further on their meanings;
I disparage the conventional maxims of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius,
and I deride the renowned principles of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
