By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to produce ten copies of each.
He distributed [the scriptures] to various temples, entrusting them to be circulated together.
Having followed the example of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) in transforming the world through the ten virtuous paths,
he prohibited all acts of slaughter throughout the markets within his realm.
He issued a general prohibition throughout the countryside, forbidding the slaughter of animals.
In the regions south of the Yangtze River, military outposts were established to catch fish;
this was the case in more than thirty prefectures, everywhere alike.
One must break the dam before one can take [the fish];
yet what is taken is but a single branch compared to the forest of Deng,
while those who die in vain exceed the number of billions of sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, he bestowed his compassionate grace and abolished all [burdensome] practices.
Moreover, as the harvests were abundant and the times peaceful, the land within the seas enjoyed prosperity.
He also ordained three thousand monks and nuns, distributing them among the various provinces.
Thereupon, his virtue moved the profound mystery, and his resonance reached the Supreme Sage.
The seven calamities were simultaneously extinguished, and the seven blessings arrived in full measure;
his grace permeated the reaches beyond the nine boundaries of the earth.
His majesty extended beyond the eight extremities of the universe.
In the first month of winter that year, the barbarian king Xielì and others led their ministers and sons, bringing along their entire tribes.
Carried in swaddling clothes on their backs, they vied with one another to hasten forward, following one after another like footsteps.
Gazing longingly toward the palace courtyard, they arrived from every corner of the land to pay homage at the Heavenly Gate and entreat for their lives.
By establishing a guesthouse for the surrendered tribes, harmony was fostered through shared meals;
thus, there was no need to trouble the armies of Wei and Huo,
as their nests and lairs were naturally exhausted.
Without needing to rely on the vast armies of Emperor Xuan-yuan,
he will roll up the fugitives like a mat; thus,
the region south of the Han River shall no longer suffer the anxiety of intermingling with barbarian tribes.
The northern borders have ceased the incursions of the powerful Hu tribes;
the regions of Ma'an and Longdui have already been bathed in the winds of the Tang.
From the banks of the Jiao River to the shores of the Clear Sea, all have become sacred lands.
How peaceful! How peaceful!
We rejoice together on this day;
free from worldly toil and affairs,
we share in celebration this very morning.
His achievement in unifying heaven and establishing the ultimate standard stands alone as preeminent throughout antiquity;
his practice of honoring the Buddha and revering goodness surpasses that of all former sages.
His Majesty once faced him on the battlefield with blades drawn;
yet upon ascending the throne, his heart was filled with deep affection,
and he consequently issued an imperial decree.
At every site where an army had been stationed, a temple was established;
the relevant authorities were tasked with providing all necessary supplies to ensure they were fully prepared.
In total, ten such sites were established throughout the realm.
It is solemn and dignified, worthy of admiration.
Furthermore, in the past, while personally visiting the South Mountain to escape the summer heat,
[the Emperor] selected this sacred site and initiated this magnificent construction.
As for its terrain:
it borders the vast expanse of the Qin River and adjoins the azure heights of the Long Mountains.
To the east, it bathes in the waves where the sun emerges;
to the west, it overlooks the bay where the moon hangs suspended.
The phoenix perches upon the stone of *qiongqi*.
Dense and towering, they pierce the heavens;
dragon-encircling cliffs of grotesque wonder;
vaulting and arched, they thrust toward the Milky Way.
Not only do the craggy pines pierce the sun,
but the valley bamboos also brush against the clouds;
it is truly the place where the Four Recluses cultivated their virtue.
It was originally a stronghold established by the three states of Qin;
it was abandoned by Emperor Taizu and converted into a monastery,
thereby increasing its auspicious significance.
For this reason, it was called Longtian (Dragon Field).
He also sent six *jiaju* (lacquered cloth) statues of the same size as Emperor Taizu and the Prince-in-Chief,
to be permanently enshrined and venerated there.
The necessities for the great assembly were supplied by the officials without the labor of purchasing land, nor was it necessary to wait for the scattering of gold.
The fragrance of the harmonious wind against the grain filled the courtyard in dense abundance.
Auspicious and supple grasses spread luxuriantly,
trailing down the steps,
for the sake of the Great Empress Mu.
At Qingshanguan, he constructed Cide Temple,
adorned with various ornaments of *cintāmaṇi* jewels and Jāmbūnada gold, each one exquisitely magnificent.
Although he knew that what had been accomplished was rare and marvelous, he still said that it was beyond measure and yet remained unexpressed.
In the sixth year, during the middle summer month, at the Inner Zhen'an Ward west of the Tai City wall, [he passed away].
For Empress Mu, he further constructed Hongfu Monastery.
Examining its strategic topography, which embraced both the marketplace and the imperial court, he commanded the artisans to lay the foundation and erect the structures.
Hardly had the silver plaque been affixed when this golden garden was completed.
Dharma companions jostle one another shoulder-to-shoulder, while the nobility of the court crane their necks in expectation.
As for the site itself, high walls enclose the moats,
stretching for a hundred *zhì* in a winding and leisurely course.
The tiered city walls form its corners,
rising steeply through nine layers and extending far and wide; therein,
the precious monasteries were extensively opened out, fully equipped with every kind of magnificent architectural splendor.
Observing the stars and measuring the shadows, they set up the gnomon and the plumb line.
The royal shoes cast their radiance, and the golden door-knobs gleam with color.
The long corridors host the constellations, and the overhanging eaves touch the heavens.
Floating pillars and embroidered rafters display patterns of cloud-gas above;
soaring eaves and carved balustrades are adorned with rainbows below.
The shadow-towers stand solemnly facing one another.
The sutra platforms stand in majestic parallel tiers,
exhausting the proportions of vermilion and azure and exhausting the marvelous beauty of floral patterns and embroidery.
Its exquisite beauty surpasses that of celestial immortals, and its spiritual power exhausts the depths of ghosts and spirits.
Golden platters receive the dew,
rivaling the jade trees of the Ganshui Palace.
Jewel bells harmonize with the gentle breeze,
depicting the Jambūnada grove in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing;
sparse bells pierce the night, and pure chants rise in the morning.
Its rhythms harmonize with the echoes of Mount Yushan,
and its resonance accords with the spirit of Longmu; it is a place where numinous wonders find refuge and where meditative wisdom relies for support.
The definitive meaning and the stilling of the mind reside herein.
The Great Chancellor of Wei, Prince of Bohai, possessed a spiritual vitality and a natural endowment of extraordinary refinement.
His virtue encompasses both civil and martial arts;
his talents span ritual and music.
He is a vessel worthy of the state’s altars and its jade insignia.
Possessing the talent of a pillar for the court and the state,
he truly embodies the spirit of a royal assistant;
all acclaim him as the one entrusted with pacifying the world’s turmoil.
As for turning the heart toward and submitting to the Way,
he alone surpassed his contemporaries;
he was not stingy with even elephants and horses.
There were no pearls or jewels [offered] out of affection. At Dingguo Monastery, a precious stupa was constructed by the seven princes on the right:

the Wei State Councilor, Grand Protector, and Duke of Sibu, Prince Yi-ryeol of Guangyang; the Wei Prince Zhongwu of Guangyang; the Wei Duke of Sibu, Prince of Guangyang; the Wei Prince Wenxian of Guangyang; the Wei Chancellor, Prince Gao; the Wei Prince of Runan; and the Wei Prince of Yidu.
They harbored reverent faith within their hearts and made its diligent cultivation their primary vocation;
whether in civil or military affairs, they assisted the state and protected their families.
They possessed the integrity of a pillar and foundation stone, and were endowed with the virtue required for the imperial court.
One perceives how empty clouds change abruptly and recognizes that the vapors of a mirage are not permanent; thus,
one awakens to the realization that one's own body likewise returns to total extinction.
They then turned their minds toward the principles of the Buddha and together followed the holy transformation;
all received the eight precepts and observed the six days of fasting,
building temples, ordaining monks, and holding assemblies to honor the good.
Mu, Prince of Shangdang of the Wei, and Ji, Prince of Changshan of the Wei—these two princes:
Mu was gentle and magnanimous by nature and possessed a handsome appearance;
Ji had a majestic and imposing countenance, with a waist girth of ten spans.
He was upright by nature, dignified and refined, speaking little and maintaining purity and circumspection.
He constantly stayed within the inner palace gates;
even during the heat of summer, he would not remove his robes or cap.
He served as high official up to the rank of Grand Guardian (Shizhong) and Commander-in-Chief (Dasi-ma).
Wei Huaiyang Wang Wei, Wei Hedong Wang Xun, Wei Dongyang Wang Pi, and Wei Huainan Wang Ta—Wei, Xun, Pi, and Ta—all possessed magnificent and imposing physiques.
He had large ears and prominent eyebrows.
For forty years, during the six fast days of the three long months, he observed the precepts and maintained the fasts without fail.
At that time, he recited the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
He founded Fawang Temple.
Being advanced in years and of great reputation, he came to court leaning on a staff;
yet his voice remained clear and resonant.
He possessed extensive knowledge of state affairs;
there was nothing he did not know when questioned.
Furthermore, during banquets and feasts, he always took his seat at the head of the table.
Whenever he discussed and savored the principles of the Buddha with princes, scholars, great virtuous ones, and renowned monks,
he would raise his voice and speak loudly to the assembly, saying:
"The Buddhist teachings are profound and harmonious."
This is not something known by the Confucians or the Mohists.
King Han of Wei was well-versed in the affairs of his time and fully understood the principles of success and failure.
He attended to immediate matters while planning for the distant future; he prepared for all contingencies even in moments of haste.
He esteemed benevolence and practiced righteousness.

Respected by both the court and the commonalty were Wei Minister of Education Prince Xiang of Beihai and Minister of Works Prince Yong of Gaoyang; whether by descent from the imperial branch or by status as members of the maternal kin, they held the essential levers of governance.
Bearing the weight of the Divine Land,
they were both moved by the perfect pearl;
they admired and encouraged their own minds.
While he administered the affairs of state with a formal brilliance, proclaiming the Way of governance,
he maintained an open mind toward Buddhist principles and held profound faith in the Bridge of Dharma.
He commissioned the carving of statues, the transcription of scriptures, and the establishment of pagodas and monasteries.
He transcribed all twelve collections of the sutras.
Prince Xiao Xie of Pengcheng of the Wei dynasty exhausted his heart and mind to protect the late Emperor (Shizong).
From internal and external exhortations up to the ascending and establishing [of the Dharma],
the gates of the Dharma were grandly opened and Buddhist activities flourished extensively.
He renovated monasteries and constructed sacred stupas.
Wen Ruofeng of Waijinan was elegant and refined in his character.
His deportment was composed and dignified;
his speech was profound and beautiful;
his words and countenance were calm and harmonious.
At that time, people composed a verse about him, saying:
"The three dukes are all elegant and refined like fine jade,
yet none compare to the one from Ji'nan, who fulfills his office with such integrity."
As for orally reciting the golden words and mentally aspiring to uphold the Pure Kings,
one should observe the fast and eat vegetarian food.
In protecting the Dharma and revering the Sangha,
nothing can surpass this.
Wei Anfeng Wang Yanming and Zhongshan Wang Xi were both members of the imperial clan who were erudite in antiquity and accomplished in literature.
He established a ritual site for both meditation and preaching, maintaining them in continuous succession.
Using ink mixed with fragrant liquid,
he transcribed one hundred copies of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
A copy of the *Suśruta-śāstra* in golden characters and one volume of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*,
both contained within caskets made of four precious substances and encased in chambers of five fragrant woods;
these were to be used for the practice of the Way through pure fasting during tranquil nights and auspicious seasons.
Every time he emitted divine light of five colors that illuminated the halls and buildings,
everyone beheld it together and their resolve to cultivate the path redoubled.
Wang Song of Langya during the Wei dynasty had mastered the Six Classics.
Shi Gai was among the most eminent of the hundred clans;
his attire, demeanor, and bearing were esteemed by both the court and the commonalty.
His lofty discourse and pure character stood alone, transcending his contemporaries.
When he reached the age of twenty, he was invited as a guest. Emperor Wu of Liang marveled at him and conversed with him all day long.
Emperor Wu said to him:
In the past, Wang Ling served under the Han,
and Jiang Wei governed Shu;
in each place they reached renown.
Why need one necessarily be from the native land for such treatment to be accorded?
His constant correspondence with Emperor Wu of Liang invariably began with the words:
"Sung, Prince of Linhuai of the Wei."
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty did not reproach him;
rather, he held him in great esteem and respect.
On the days of the six fasts, he would invariably prepare pure offerings for the Buddha and provide meals for the monastic community.
The stipends he received were mostly spent on Buddhist scriptures and images.
Jia, the Prince of Guangyang and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat under the Wei dynasty, never showed signs of either joy or anger;
he was profound, prudent, and fond of learning.
He was benevolent, kind, and profoundly filial, never wavering even in moments of urgency.
He read all the sutras three times in total.
He constructed Aijingsi Temple to repay the grace of the two emperors.
He compiled fifteen fascicles of excerpts from various sutras;
with his heart surrendered and his life entrusted [to the Dharma],
his resolve was fixed upon the Citadel of the Law.
The Wei Prince of Chenliu, Qian, possessed a majestic and imposing bearing.
His physical strength was peerless.
Having entered the monastic life since childhood, he cultivated his mind with sincerity, yearning for the Way.
Thereafter, although he returned to lay life, he did not abandon his practice of the Truth.
Though he engaged in secular affairs, he remained deeply devoted to his superior religious vocation.
Emperor Xianwu of the Wei and Qi dynasties wished for him to follow the mysterious destiny [of the dharma].
His wisdom and spiritual practice are profound;
his benevolence is like spring,
and his majesty is like summer.
Be sincere toward all things and let the Great Way permeate the eight directions;
cultivate the mind and overcome the self.
Dedicating [the merit] toward the True Dharma, he constructed the Great Compassion Temple to universally save all living beings.

The Wei Envoys—General-in-Chief of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad, Prince Qi; Wei Jurlu Wang Chan; Wei Lu Shangshu Shi, Prince Pengcheng Shao; Wei Qiaojun Wang Liang; Wei Jiangxia Wang Yi; and Wei Lintao Wang Rong—all were heroic, resolute, and preeminent.
His character was peerless;
yet he placed his faith in the words of the Dharma and dedicated himself to the teachings of Śākyamuni.
Feng Xi, the Grand Preceptor, Grand Marshal, and Regional Inspector of Luozhou, was the elder brother of Empress Dowager Wenming.
With the utmost faith in the Buddha,
he constructed stupas and monasteries throughout the various provinces,
numbering seventy-two in total.
He transcribed sixteen sets of the entire Buddhist canon and frequently engaged in scholarly discussions on the Buddha’s teachings with renowned monks. Hu Guozhen,
the Grand Master (Situ) and Governor of Youzhou who held the rank of Commander-in-Chief (Shichie), was the father of Empress Dowager Ling.
One should solely attend to ritual purity,
diligently engage in prostrations,
copy scriptures, and fashion images.
He founded Zhenghua Temple and made offerings to a hundred monks.

Zu Ying, styled Yuanzhen, was the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial during the Wei dynasty; he was endowed with abundant blessings and virtue, and his spirit was nurtured by accumulated goodness.
His character was spacious and tranquil;
his intellect was enlightened and awakened;
his speech possessed the eloquence of the Blue Cock.
Holding in his hand the inscribed dragon-patterned vessel,
he was thus entrusted with the treasury of meaning and the profound source of the Way.
Li Wuweī, the Minister of Works of the Wei Dynasty, followed his innate nature and stood apart from the crowd;
he acted spontaneously according to his own principles,
probing the profound and reaching the far-reaching.
Possessing refinement within and embodying innate substance,
like a great swan about to take flight,
he immediately harbors the ambition for the four seas.
As a fine steed begins its gallop,
it already possesses the heart for a thousand-li journey;
though state affairs are numerous and extensive, [he remains focused].
He constantly took the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* as his primary practice,
observing the six monthly fasts throughout his life without ever neglecting them.
Li Shí, the Prince of Changning and Grand Tutor of the Wei dynasty, was upright and correct in his personal conduct.
He was pure and frugal in his conduct. He was careful in concluding his undertakings and diligent in initiating them.
He upheld the Dharma and revered his teachers.
He never neglected the six fast days and constantly observed the five precepts.
Dou Lue, the Minister of the Guards and Duke of Jianchang of the Wei dynasty, naturally possessed the magnanimity of Yi Yin and Hou He.
Having long cherished the resolve to serve as a pillar of state,
he was entrusted with the mandate to lead an expedition;
thus, he discerned the deceptive emptiness of the enemy's fox-like defenses.
When exercising authority over adversaries,
one must discern the shifting directions of the winds and clouds;
though wealthy, remain free from arrogance.
Though noble, he was free from arrogance;
with reverent faith and profound veneration, he entrusted his life to the World Hero.
He founded the two monasteries of Ling-shan and Fa-yun.
He made offerings to approximately two hundred monks.
Cao Zuo, the Minister of the Interior of the Wei dynasty, possessed courage that surpassed his peers and military strategy that exceeded the world.
Wei’s Minister of Education Gao Longzhi possessed a transcendent spirit that surpassed his peers;
his virtuous influence was worthy of emulation.
Wei’s Palace Attendant and Grand Chancellor Yuan Yi was preeminent in both his vital energy and physical stature.
His refined brilliance was pure and serene;
he served as a ceremonial ornament to both the court and the commonalty, and his contributions in providing counsel and support were widely renowned.
He founded Fayin Temple in Daizhou.
Murong Shaozong, the Right Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Commissioner of the Taiwei, was renowned for his sagacity and discernment;
he was profoundly devoted to honoring the worthy.
Xing Luan, the Minister of Personnel under the Wei dynasty, founded Pujisi Temple. He possessed refined regulations and elegant conversation;
he enjoyed the subtle flavors of the *Xuan* and *Zhuang* [Laozi and Zhuangzi] and the *Shi* and *Sao* [poetry].
He revered the Mahāyāna, commissioning the creation of statues and the establishment of monasteries.
Lu Zhengping, General of the Flying Cavalry of Wei, Grand Marshal with the same rank as the Minister of Education, and Regional Inspector of Hengzhou, was upright and impartial.
He adhered to the Way and possessed few desires,
maintaining the noble character of one who excels in benevolence.
He possessed a refined and elegant countenance;
reciting the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* as the basis for his discourses,
none among the people of that time dared to challenge him in debate due to his noble character.
He was the second son of Lu Zai.
Zheng Qiong, the Duke Gong and Grand Master of Ceremonies under the Wei dynasty, praised his virtue in an inscription:
"With jade of the finest quality as his heart."
A high official of the court and a model for human relations,
he founded Jingyu Monastery and constructed the Fahua Hall.
He maintained monthly vegetarian feasts and regularly commissioned the copying of sacred images each year.
Han Zhongxiang, the Governor of Yongzhou during the Wei dynasty, founded Hanshijun Temple, which was simple yet refined and spacious.
Distinguishing between the refined and the vulgar,
he harbored a profound sense of detachment from the self.
During the Wei dynasty, Cui Ling, a Gentleman of the Palace Gate, established Baoen Temple and devoted his mind to the arts of the Way.
He entrusted his aspirations to the Odes and Histories;
he refined them with calligraphy and composition, and through chiseling and polishing, he perfected his virtue.
Having heard of your reputation, my empty thoughts are stirred; gazing upon your excellence, my heart is inclined toward you.
You stand alone as the preeminent figure of the age.
As the foremost among beings,
he dedicated himself to the Triple Gem and committed his life to the Four Great Vows.
Within the city of Ye, he established Ba'en Temple.
Lu Lingshou, the Regional Inspector of Youzhou during the Wei dynasty, established Tongxuan Temple. His inner virtue was as refined as jade, while his external demeanor was as solemn as a gale;
his character and capacity were profound and elegant.
The Divine employed his lofty brilliance to construct Tongxuan Temple in Youzhou,
providing offerings for one hundred monks.

Zhao Yuantuo, the Governor of Pei Commandery during the Wei dynasty, was imbued with the essence of the celestial bodies and endowed with the spiritual numen of the rivers and mountains; from his youth,
his reputation was preeminent and his excellence renowned.
Renowned since his early twenties,
his resolve in faith and reverence remained unshakable,
and his mind of generosity and forbearance never exhausted.
Transcribing scriptures and fashioning images does not weary the mind.

Li Jiang, Duke of Wuyi and Governor of Henan during the Wei dynasty, constructed Maitreya Temple; its ceremonial regalia and cultural accoutrements were so magnificent that the carriages and canopies seemed to stretch endlessly before one’s eyes.
Guarding the One and embracing the True,
with their aspirations set upon the Land of Peaceful Nurturing,
during the months of the three long days.
He would certainly observe a fast of purification;
on the anniversary of his parents' deaths,
he remained in profound grief until dawn.
He built the Maitreya Monastery and provided offerings to one hundred monks.
Lu Zai, who served as the Palace Attendant to the Heir Apparent and Censor-in-Chief under the Wei dynasty, was originally a native of Wu.
He served as the military commander-in-chief (xingjun dudu) for Yi-zhen, the Prince of Xiangyang of the Song dynasty.
Later, after falling into the hands of Helian,
he entered the service of the Wei.
Possessing talent and eloquence,
he was highly esteemed by the nobility of the Wei court;
yet by nature, he cherished solitude and tranquility.
He constantly took the Buddha-dharma as his primary concern.
Every time he read the various scriptures, he praised their profound tenets.
In the final years of his life, he became so refined and focused that the characters in the sutras emitted light.
He recited the Lotus Sutra orally,
at which time he was moved by the appearance of śarīra relics.
Xu Bo Tao, the Wei-era Minister of the Guard, possessed the spirit of long-standing benevolence.
He propagated the way of unyielding friendship and revered the True Dharma without fail throughout his time.

Wen Zisheng, the Court Gentleman for Mounted Attendants of the Wei dynasty, possessed the literary style of Sima Xiangru’s *Three Capitals* and the talent of Yang Xiong who submitted his works a hundred times;
his compositions put even brocade and embroidery to shame.
King Jin was humbled by its radiant brilliance;
he venerated the Sublime Dharma and took delight in the Mahāyāna.
Houmochen Yin, General of the Far Reaches (Neiyuan Jiangjun) of the Wei, founded Zhiyuan Temple. He was a descendant of Prince Jing of Zhongshan of the Han dynasty;
since the Han period, his lineage had established the state of Feng.
He took the name of his fief as his clan name and was thus styled Chen (Cín).
He constructed the Jetavana Monastery and other edifices.
The monastery constantly maintained vegetarian feasts and lectures,
as well as almsgiving to the field of compassion;
those mentioned previously were all eminent figures from the Wei dynasty.
I have outlined the general features of the eminent and talented men of this age who revered the Buddha’s teachings. Prince Chak,

the Grand Chancellor of the Great Qi State and Commander-in-Chief of both Internal and External Military Affairs, Duke of Changshan, possessed a legacy of merit and virtue that was lofty and magnificent.
Teda Chaolun (Qi Taiguo Lanling Wang Changgong) was exceptionally intelligent and surpassed his peers;
both the court and the commonalty respected and feared him. Qisitu Langyao Wang Yan assisted and praised the imperial house.
Guanglong served as the Director of the Imperial Secretariat and was a pillar of the royal house under Emperor Zhizheng.

Guangping Prince Zhi, who served as the Great Commander-in-Chief and Director of the Imperial Secretariat under Emperor Xiaowu, possessed wisdom that transcended his peers. His civil and military regulations were exemplary.
Cao Li was warm and upright; his conduct was as excellent and profound as that of Danyue, Prince of Qinghe, Grand Marshal of the Qi.
Guangfeng was robust and far-reaching; his character was as discerning and profound as that of Xiaoyan, Prince of Guangning, Left Vice Director of the Qi.

Tang Yong, Prince of Jinchang, Duke of Chang'an, of the Great Zhongzheng Commandery; a man of upright integrity who brought his life to a noble end, serving as Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, Registrar of the Department of State Affairs, Commander-in-Chief with Imperially Commissioned Authority, General of the Flying Cavalry, Grand Master of Ceremonies with the Rank of the Third Order, General of the Household, Governor of Zhaozhou, concurrently serving as Metropolitan Commander of the Six Prefectures and Governor of Bingzhou.
He constructed the Great Ningguo Temple, Adorned with the Multitude of Meanings,
and cast a single gilded statue of Maitreya; these were like auspicious portents of celestial phenomena and divine signs.
The mountain deity bestows blessings upon this flourishing age;
he manifests supreme virtue and has served five sovereigns, receiving the honor of the eighth rank of enfeoffment.
He attended the Emperor’s carriage when going forth and stepped upon the green mats when entering the palace;
he collected what was omitted and supplemented what was deficient.
To present what is correct and replace what is incorrect is the fundamental principle of military organization;
it is the secret of the military tally and the precious treasure of the state.
It must not be shown to others;
it is that to which the heart and backbone turn for refuge.
It is guarded by the corpse and held in the utmost secrecy.
Furthermore, he was charged with investigating and supervising the grain tribute;
he oversaw the entire state of Zhao,
wielding his ceremonial staff to extend his majesty and authority.
Descending from his carriage, he distributed kindness;
the powerful and wealthy, who had previously practiced兼并 (monopolization and annexation), folded their hands in submission upon catching sight of his stern demeanor.
Weak and marginalized, we were on the verge of being cast down;
now, bathed by the dew and rain of imperial grace, we find respite.
With golden lips and wooden tongues, [the Emperor] guides our ears and points out our palms.
When clothing and food are abundant, one understands honor and disgrace;
when rites and music are pervasive, one recognizes loyalty and filial piety.
At the roadside taverns, the goods of extraordinary trade have ceased.
The officials of Yuantù possessed a sense of compassion and pity;
their restraint was as pure as fish in water and their integrity as clear as water being drawn from a spring.
The high officials of Cānxū revered them as if they were divine beings.
The common people of the rural villages looked up to him as they do to the sun and moon.
Furthermore, with excellent fields abiding in his person and true gold inherent in his nature, he sported among all dharmas, tamed his faculties,
and practiced diligently upon hearing the teachings.
Upon seeing this, he immediately rejoiced;
for the sake of the nation and its common people,
[he established it] in the ancient capital of Yao.
He constructed the Zongyi Zhuangyan Monastery,
modeled after the grandeur of the *Dazhuang* hexagram; its proportions were measured according to the celestial patterns of the *Gengui*.
The tablet is placed upon the mourning altar;
turning its back to the shade and facing the sun,
it receives warmth from the cold.
The lunar palace and solar hall shed their radiant light day and night;
the Nala garden and lotus pedestal manifest different aspects through spring and autumn.
Renowned monks follow one another in succession, and those of pure faith stand side by side in solidarity.
On auspicious days of the month, people vied with one another to offer prostrations.
Furthermore, he constructed Danning Guosi Temple at Yangping;
its precious edifice rose loftily above the earth.
The refined hermitage stands remote and magnificent;
its rafters are fashioned from *wén-xìng* wood, and its pillars are made of *cān-dān*.
Adorned with intricate patterns, they radiate a brilliant luster.
Crimson and green hues reflected off one another.
Furthermore, he cast a single golden image of Maitreya,
seven feet in height including its radiance.
Two statues of Zhang Ba (eight chi) made of white stone,
along with more than three thousand scrolls of the entire Buddhist canon,
and approximately ten thousand repaired ancient statues.
The Right Chancellor of Qi, Prince of Xianyang Hu Lü Mingyue, possessed a courage that was unsurpassed;
his integrity remained steadfast even in adversity. The Left Chancellor of Qi, Prince of Pingyuan Duan Xiaoxian, was diligent and devoted to the affairs of state.

Yunfu served as Vice Director of the Secretariat under the Qi dynasty; He Shikai, Prince of Huainan, was sincere, prudent, diligent, and reverent, strengthening himself in the service of the law; Gao Yue, Prince of Qinghe, Grand Master of Ceremonies of Qi, was courageous, capable, pure, and elegant; Kudici Qianqiu, Prince of Zhangwu, Grand Chancellor of Qi, was fierce and resolute yet respectful and compliant; Gao Yangui, Prince of Qin, Palace Attendant of Qi, was broad-minded and gracious; and Yuan Luo, Palace Attendant and Director of the Secretariat, was noble and refined.
Scholars of talent and renown,
such as Wang Yuanjing and Xing Zicai, all served as his guests;
nevertheless, he was by nature frugal and simple.
He was gentle and courteous in his dealings with others.
He venerated the Triple Gem and held the Four Great Vows in high esteem.
At Faxi Temple, he constructed a seven-story brick pagoda.
As for exhausting one's heart to assist the sagely sovereign and cultivating oneself to plan for eternal peace,
this brings tranquility to the ruler above.
It provides security for oneself below;
it is indeed a water-mirror for human relations and a model for all under heaven.

Gao Zhao, Director of the Imperial Secretariat of the Qi dynasty, founded the Xianju Nunnery. Peng Le, Grand Marshal of the Qi dynasty, was renowned for his benevolence and generosity. Pan Xiang, Minister of Education of the Qi dynasty, was noble in character and esteemed for his righteousness. Sima Ziru, Minister of Works of the Qi dynasty, was distinguished for his pure and elegant scholarship and his austere integrity. Yang Zunyan, Court Gentleman for Ceremonial and Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat of the Qi dynasty, was noted for his warm and perceptive mind.
His dignified bearing was forceful and elegant;
early on he displayed the luster of jade,
and from youth he possessed the resonance of metal.
His civil governance encompassed the ninefold merits,
and his military prowess embraced the seven virtues;
he spread his magnificent reputation throughout the world.
He moved the hearts of joy throughout the realm;
as Prince Wenxuan, he looked down from the capital with lofty vision,
while the Vice President of the Secretariat oversaw all affairs of state.
With bellies drummed and ram blocks struck, the people raised no sounds of resentment;
within ten years, the state of Qi was greatly governed.
To the power of unifying through rectification, Master Yang contributed.
He had extensively studied both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings,
was proficient in both Confucianism and Buddhism, and [lived near] temples that stood as closely packed as the teeth of a comb.
Pagodas stand facing one another;
the assembly of Dharma practitioners extends in continuous ranks;
men and women alike turn their merit toward enlightenment.
He guarded and sustained [the teachings] with his whole heart;
the people all looked up to him from near at hand.
Qi Shaofu, Shangshu Puye, and Weimu were thoroughly proficient in ritual and music.
He synthesized the fundamental principles of human relations,
profoundly realized the truths of suffering and emptiness,
and held the True Dharma in the highest esteem.
His learning encompassed the traditions of Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan,
and his talent surpassed those of Ying Yong and Liu Xie.
He was equal in brilliance to Cui Xian, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Vice Director of the Secretariat, who had received the mandate to assist in founding the dynasty.
His favor was second only to those of the two southern dynasties;
indeed, he was an object of universal gaze for the court, and his status and reputation were paramount among the human relations of the age.
He also placed his faith in the Buddha-dharma,
extensively established fields of merit,
and delighted in engaging in profound discourse on ultimate principles with renowned monks and transcribing the sutras.

He constructed images, repaired monasteries, and restored *gālayas*. Cui Jishu, Right Vice-Director of the Chancellery, was of pure and lofty reputation, serving as a ceremonial ornament to his generation. Yan Zijing, Left Vice-Director of the Chancellery, served those above and assisted those below, upholding the law with self-reliance. Zhao Yanshen, Director of the Chancellery, was benevolent, generous, pure, and conscientious. Hu Lü Xiaqing, Palace Attendant, possessed a sense of righteousness and valor that surpassed the world. Hu Si Wenruo, Palace Attendant, was frugal and austere, maintaining strict decorum. Xu Zhicai, Palace Attendant, followed the path of moral influence and promoted the worthy. Gao Zhengde, Palace Attendant, was upright and restrained, never wavering from his principles. Wang Yuanjing, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, was renowned for his purity and intelligence from an early age. Cui Ang, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was devoted to righteousness and esteemed for benevolence; he was a distinguished clan of high standing in the court. Liu Ti, Attendant Cavalier-in-Ordinary, was a scholar whose learning encompassed the *Qilüe* (Seven Compendia).
The four gates were recently manifested. Du Bi, Minister of the Court of Palace Attendants of the Qi dynasty, was worthy of praise for his resolute character;
his words and deeds were consistently trustworthy. Xing Zicai, Palace Secretary of the Qi dynasty, possessed a brilliance that shone like flowing light.

Qi Wen was a man whose writings surpassed the world; Zu Xiaozheng, the Secretariat Director of the Qi dynasty, possessed abundant learning and a literary talent that illuminated his age; Feng Xiaoyan, the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs under the Qi, was as lofty and far-reaching as a pure breeze.

At that time, Fan Ru—the foremost among those held in high esteem, a Commander-in-Chief with the rank of Pacifying the South General, Acting Governor of Renzhou, Grand Master of Imperial Honors of the Fifth Rank (Jinzi Guanglu Dafu), and Marquis of Ankang—constructed two monasteries, Zhulin and Baku, whose architectural forms were harmonious and their interiors profound.
His intellectual insight was clear and lucid;
his sincerity and noble ambition were peerless.
He founded Zhulin Temple in Luzhou.
He founded Bakgo Temple in Inju and dedicated himself to the creation of statues and the transcription of scriptures year after year without ceasing.
He was a preeminent talent of the Qi dynasty and a distinguished figure of the Northern Dynasties.
They were all scholars who mastered both ancient and modern learning, penetrating the profound mysteries of both Buddhism and Confucianism;
they possessed deep faith in the Buddhist gate and a clear understanding of cause and effect,
personally unrolling the jade-axled scriptures and orally reciting the golden words, and their assembly was vast.
They are like grasses and trees relying upon the great earth;
their concealment is like that of scaly creatures floating upon a vast river.
As for those commoners in white-walled cottages and nameless elderly peasants who possess a slight understanding,
aspire with rare devotion, and have developed even a small measure of faith,
they are beyond counting.
How could one dare to speak otherwise?
Thus, blessings shall be bestowed upon the four modes of birth and prosperity shall flow throughout the three worlds;
may benevolence and forbearance extend to both sons and grandsons.
There is no virtue that he is unable to practice to its full extent. Zhou Zhuguo,
the Prince of Wei and Governor-General of Xiangzhou, established Fenglin Temple to plant the roots of manifold merits.
In Xiangzhou, he renovated Fenglin Temple;
perched on precipices and spanning valleys, its rafters joined the clouds.
Fragrant pavilions and meditation cells were built upon the crags and ledges of the cliffs.
The Buddhist rites are solemn and orderly, and the temple buildings are radiant with splendor.
The moon enters the autumn windows, and the breeze arises at the summer doors; forgetfulness of sorrow fills the entire courtyard.
Chang-le towers over the steps;
bamboo rises beside the thatched eaves;
pines stretch across the stone terraces.
Extraordinary peaks stretch across the sun;
lofty trees pierce the heavens.
To set one's eyes upon them brings clarity to the mind.
Spontaneously forgetting his way back home,
Zhou Zhuguo, the Prince of Zhao and Governor-General of Yizhou, built Huiyan Temple and took refuge in this sanctuary of benevolence.
The Left Governor of Yizhou also built Huiyan Temple.
The heavy gates span the distance, and soaring pavilions reach the clouds.
Birds perch upon them like dragons coiling;
phoenixes soar as if scales join one another.
The windows open like the lightning of a divine maiden, and the beams reflect the rainbow of a beauty.
The eaves slope downward on all four sides, overlooking the courtyard, while the steps rise directly upward in three stages.
Golden cords demarcate the paths.
He further planned the gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
canopies were draped along the steps,
immediately depicting the lands of Udyāna.
In this auspicious month of the third spring and on this propitious day of the eighth seasonal node,
men and women, both those of the capital and the provinces, as well as the faithful and the chivalrous, [gathered together].
He surrendered himself in devotion, turning his merit toward [the Buddha] and prostrating in refuge.

Prince Qi, the Zhou Zhuguo and Governor of Yongzhou, founded Anju Monastery; the Grand Preceptor and Chief Minister of Zhou, the Zhuguo Dajiangjun and Duke of Jin, Yuwen Hu, founded Huitong Monastery. The Duke’s territory was within the domain of Wen and Zhao; his fame was as lofty as that of Kings Shan and Yao.
He received the bundled *mao* grass from the four states that had submitted,
and monopolized the power of military expeditions over the five marquises.
When King Wen of Zhou served as his minister, all administrative achievements flourished.
Gao Yao provided counsel such that the world was free from affairs;
the altars of the land and grain were established through him,
and the court relied upon him for its impartial administration.
Possessing profound faith that set him apart from the crowd and an incomparable dedication to the path,
he caused the Image-Teaching to flourish and established benevolent shrines.
In total, he constructed five temples, including those for the Dharma-King Maitreya, Zhigui Hui, and others.
The provision of baths and lodgings was withdrawn from his stipend, thus sparing the treasury's resources;
the rent of the commanderies and kingdoms was reduced.
There is no need for the laborious task of launching boats;
it is the site of the Precious Cauldron in Fenyin and the foundation of the Purple Palace in Anyi.
The gardens opened with the gold of the elder;
the springs gushed forth from the mendicant’s staff.
All the wood of Da Qin was exhausted, and the fire-jade of Jiaozhi could not be tilted.
The craftsmanship reaches its ultimate limit,
not following the designs of a master artisan;
the ingenuity is perfected through divine power.
Just as they were awaiting the response of Youyu,
the Celestial Treasure Stupa stood afar,
overlooking the Terrace for Divining Qi.
The numinous shrine sprang forth from the earth,
facing the slope of the Salt-Cart Pass; there,
the four assemblies observed the precepts during the two periods of the summer retreat.
He constantly turned the Wheel of Dharma and perpetually dwelt in meditative chambers.
Furthermore, he made offerings at Chonghua Temple.
Doulu Ning, the Zhou State Pillar, Minister of the Interior, and Duke of Chu,
built Luohan Temple and Huizong Temple after the death of Emperor Wenming of the Yan dynasty, Murong Huang.
His grandfather, Shiwen, was the Attendant-in-Waiting and Director of the Office of Slaves for the Chenghuang Emperor.
His father, Du, was the General of the Household and Grand Marshal, Duke of Fuling.
At the beginning of the Ning era, [Ning] was barely past the age of twenty.
When he first began his official career,
the crescent of his brow was hailed as extraordinary,
and the essence of the stars manifested his virtue.
He served in the military for thirty-seven years and personally participated in forty-two battles;
the Hu troops did not dare to graze southward.
How could a man of Zhao ever be willing to fish in the east?
Though he was a water-mirror for human relations and a cedar or cypress of his age,
he harbored universal love in his heart and made the practice of dedication his vocation.
He established the two monasteries of Luohanhui and Zong.
He cast images and transcribed scriptures in an uninterrupted succession.

Dou Chi—the Grand Marshal of the Zhou, the General of State Affairs, the Second Senior Duke, and the Marquis of Deng—was a member of a clan preeminent among the Five Tombs and of noble stock from the Three Commanderies. He founded the two monasteries of Baima and Fanyun.
Mengjin was called the Gate of Shared Virtue;
Xianyang was the assistant who first scaled the heights.
Their merit participated in the eight instruments of governance.
He entered the rank of the Six Talismans;
his flourishing lineage was immediately peaceful, prosperous, and noble.
Formerly, he was devoted solely to the teachings of Huang-Lao.
Now, having faith in the Mahāyāna,
he established the two monasteries of Baima and Fanyun,
planting the seeds for his future emergence in the world.

Duan Yuzhi, Duke of Anfeng, was a Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief, Director of the Imperial Works, Martial Guard General, General of the Supreme Crown, General of the Household, and Grand Master for Splendid Happiness; he was the later descendant of Duan Yu and the younger son of Duan Fujun.
The world prizes elegance and refinement;
illustrious reputations follow one another in succession.
The mountains and marshes communicate their vital energy.
His appearance was pure and harmonious.
At that time, Ju Ru-tan forcibly occupied Yan and Ji;
[the Emperor] commanded him to serve as the special envoy.
He showed this to the rebellious faction,
who immediately requested to submit; thus,
he restored and strengthened friendly relations and harmony.
Whatever horses, gold, and cowries he obtained were all used for copying scriptures and bestowed upon the orphaned and the elderly.

Duke Dou Gong, the Zhou Pillar of State, Governor of Yongzhou, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Eight Provinces including Nan-yuan, and General Administrator of Yanzhou, was a descendant of a lineage as enduring as a tortoise-shell mirror, whose family of hereditary officials has flourished for generations.
The entire family reveres the Dharma, sharing in the auspicious joy of the *Heshao* music.
Yuwen Gui, Duke of Anding and General of the State of Zhou and Governor of Youzhou, was the grandson of Emperor Wen, the Founder of the Dynasty.
The son of the Prince of Qi, who served as a Zhuguo;
he was diligent in his studies at the Eastern Academy and the Western School, and remained detached from worldly scriptures.
His virtue was esteemed within the Confucian community,
his reputation was eminent in the Imperial Academy,
and he served his parents with the utmost filial piety.
He serves the Buddha with utmost reverence;
generosity and forbearance dwell within his heart,
becoming even more profound as he grows older.

Zhou Kai-fu, who held the rank of Yitong Sansi and served as the Taizixinma (Clerk for the Crown Prince), Lord of Yunningzhuang, Prince of Langyao Commandery, Tuoba Sheng, and the Zhongcheng and Taibao, Governor of Sizhou.
He was the grandson of Prince Guangyang Jia.
His father, Tong, renounced his status as the heir to the state to join the Wang family;
he changed the name of Jieshi to Xiangcheng.
He transformed Xuyang into a Nala garden;
he cast aside his crown and robes to don the garments of a farmer;
he ceased the playing of strings and songs to follow the refined Buddhist chants.
Lord Zhuang, out of filial devotion for his father, also aspired to take refuge [in the Triple Gem].
He continued to constantly cultivate pure practices within his private residence.

There was Yuwen Shangu, Duke of Hedong, serving as the Administrator of the Secretariat and Attendant-at-Horse of the Court of General Supervision for Shan Prefecture. Yuwen Shangu—his courtesy name was Shangu—was a man of the Yuwen clan.
His courtesy name was Zhongliang.
Having reached the age of maturity, he pursued his studies and inherited the teachings of a hundred masters.
Having entered the court at the age of twenty,
he galloped forward with unrestrained speed across a thousand li.
At the beginning of the Datong era, he presented the report of victory at Shayuan.
Taking up the lands of Hedong,
he took up his sword to submit with sincerity to his own clan;
together with his fellow countrymen, he attained the establishment of a state.
Possessing great faith in the True Dharma and fearing what lies ahead,
he commissioned the carving of statues and the transcription of sutras,

performing meritorious deeds throughout his life. Zhou Yanghua, Grand Master for Ceremonial and Peer of the Third Grade, was the grandson of the Great Chancellor of Wei, Prince Kang of Jingzhao, Yuan Ang.
He was the son of Tai Bao Lu Shangshu Hengzhi.
He was characterized by his mildness and reverence,
and he dwelt in his heart with benevolence and filial piety.
He traveled to study among the Confucian scholars;
having early on mastered the classics and histories, he developed a profound reverence for the teachings of Śākyamuni.
He donated his own residence to establish Choude Temple.

Yang Zuan, the Zhou Pillar of State and Grand General, Duke of Dong in Longxi; and his paternal kinsman Qiu, a high-ranking official from Henan and a noble scion of Huashan, led the three armies of the Feathered Forest Guard to train their troops at the Six Garrisons.
His father, Anren, was the Great Commander of the Northern Route and Garrison Commander of Shuozhou.
From his ancestors back, they had all revered the Buddhist faith.

Yang Cao was the Right Attendant of High Rank and Court Gentleman of the Secretariat during the Zhou Tongzhou Prefectural Governor’s tenure; he was the tenth generation of the Western Han and the fourth generation of the Eastern Han.
With vermilion wheels and flowered canopies, his lineage has been passed down through successive generations;
he is the grandson of Shangshu Zhonggong and the descendant of the Prefect of Fenzhou.
The two Yangs lived during the same era and both venerated the Buddha-dharma.
Zheng Mu, the Minister of Works of the Zhou dynasty and Marquis of Zhen, was loyal in public service and filial at home;
these virtues originated from his native heaven.
He revered the Buddha and honored the Sangha, never growing weary over time.

Zhou Shizhong, Shaofu, Governor of Jingzhao Commandery, Director of the Executive Secretariat, Grand Master of Works, Duke of Yan Commandery, Lu Jingren, and Grand Master of the Court of the Imperial Stables Jingzhi were all his younger sons.
He possessed a refined fondness for antiquities.
His family had inherited the profession of splitting firewood,
yet he applied himself to study with diligence day and night.
The world continues the teachings of the fine bow.
My three elder brothers—Jingzhao, Jingbian, and [the third]—are all preeminent scholars among the profound sages and Confucians;
they are all extensively learned and possess powerful memories, and are each capable of revising and rectifying the constitutional statutes, systems, rites, and music.
Guanzhong was called "Master" by the people;
Heshang was suspected of being Zhongni himself.
Both were praised for exhausting the depths of Buddhism, while Zhuangzi and Laozi were deemed empty and thin.
Zhou Taibao, the Pillar of State and Great General, Duke Wu of Wu, Wei-chi An, constructed Shuaiyi Temple and Xuanhua Nunnery; Xuan-yuan was born as a Sage in Xinzheng.
He originated this great source.
Changyi descended to reside by the Ruoshui River and inherited his ancestral legacy, becoming the first ruler of the Wei clan.
The Marquis of the Wei-chi clan was enfeoffed;
their official lineage was manifested through meritorious service to the state,
and the adoption of a clan name resulted from the grant of a fief.
Continuing the illustrious lineage,
the deep merits were engraved upon the ritual tripods;
the lofty foundation flourished in successive splendor.
The common vessels record his deeds and conduct:
his father was the Pillar-of-State General of the Army, Duke of Changle;
his mother was Lady Changle Dachang Mu Princess, daughter of the Minister of State.
He founded Baoyi Temple and Xuanhua Nunnery.
General Liang of the Zhou Dynasty, the Supervisor of the Southern Barbarians and Duke of Changshan, Liu Qingzhi, built Xiangshan Temple, which rises as high and steep as Mount Song.
His great hall was like clouds forming its structure;
his bearing was profound and far-reaching,
and his demeanor was composed and dignified.
He surpassed Wang Rong’s brevity and conciseness and excelled Pei Kai’s clarity and penetration;
possessing both virtue and talent, he was worthy of emulation and admiration.
In Xiangzhou, he constructed Xiangshan Temple,
its pagoda soaring above the clouds and its banners fluttering as if suspended from the heavens;
its sun-palace and lotus-terraces were magnificent.
A cluster of jewels upon a golden ground;
from afar, it resembles the Jeta Grove,
as if a copy of the Kukkutārāma.
Xi Gu, Duke Andao, was the Northern Jingzhou Inspector during the Zhou dynasty. His character was profound and steady, and his talent and strategy were versatile and effective.
He held a silver seal and a blue sash.
Having mastered the classics, he attained official rank as easily as picking up something from the ground;
his meritorious service was duly recognized,
and his virtuous conduct is recorded in the national annals.
His meritorious deeds were recorded in the family chronicles,
establishing a foundation for his lineage; thus,
for generations, his family has been illustrious.
In Dengzhou, he constructed Dewang Temple;
its chambers were refined and solemn, and its halls and pavilions were lofty and spacious.
Its location was exceptionally scenic, such that those who beheld it were moved to resolve their minds toward the path.

Xu Guo Gong Ruogan Feng, the Grand Marshal of the State of Xu, a General-in-Chief with the rank of Pillar of State holding the Imperial Seal, and Governor of Tongzhou, came to establish Zhi Sheng Temple; he was the grandson of Duke Si and the son of Duke Wu.
Establishing the state to succeed Qi,
holding the jade scepter to continue the lineage of Wei;
lofty peaks obscure the sun.
With long wings trailing through the clouds,
he constructed the Zhisheng Temple in hopes of relying upon its spiritual blessings.

The Zhou official Hou Mo Chen Xiu— holding the rank of Pacification Commissioner, Grand Tutor, Commander-in-Chief, and Duke of Qinghe— was one whose martial prowess and civil virtue were both fully realized.
He fully embodied both loyalty and filial piety;
from birth, he was mindful of goodness and constantly practiced compassion and forbearance.
At Dacheng Temple, he received the precepts and resolved his mind upon the Way.
He transcribed all the sutras and fashioned a sixteen-foot *jia-zhu* (lacquered cloth) image of Amitāyus.
All that was obtained from his stipend was offered as *dāna*.
Wei-chih Hui, Duke of Shu and Grand Preceptor of State under the Zhou dynasty, constructed Miaoxiang Temple during the chaos and turmoil of the Wei house.
He brought order to the upheavals and,
once the Zhou dynasty was established, [founded this temple].
Assisting and supporting through the rites of yielding and courtesy, his merit was lofty and his achievements weighty; wherever he was stationed,
there was nothing with which to compare him.
Revering goodness and aspiring for blessings,
his devotion became increasingly manifest over time;
he constructed Miaoxiang Temple.
The four requisites were never lacking;
the Wheel of Dharma turned constantly;
and the three trainings flourished and increased.

Anzeng Temple was built by Shi Xiong, a Grand Master of the Palace with the Rank of Peer of the State and Duke of Anzheng during the Zhou dynasty. Formerly, the Archivist (Zhou Shizhi) lingered in Zhounan and silenced himself at the Hangu Pass;
because his official title became his surname, he was subsequently known as Shi.
His grandfather, Zūn, was the Regional Inspector of Liangzhou;
his father, Níng, was the State Councilor and Duke Ānpíng of Lì.
Both possessed profound sagacity and grand strategic vision, rectifying the era and saving the world.
The family honored the Triple Gem,
and its members observed the eight precepts;
they founded Anzheng Temple to offer posthumous merit to their ancestors.

Qiu Hongbin, Duke of Anhua, General Who Pacifies the North, and Regional Inspector of Renshou during the Zhou dynasty, founded Benqi Temple. His family lineage has long been characterized by loyalty and heroism, and his clan has inherited illustrious nobility.
The alleys through which long halberds pass suggest the residence of Wang Jun; the gate,
wide enough for four horses, is grand and imposing.
He was like Wei Shu’s residence;
his younger brother, Duke Guanghua, was equally a vessel as fine as a hu or lian,
and his character was manifest as a gui or zhang jade.
A worthy elder brother and a worthy younger brother,
sharing the virtue of the late Yuan era;
some were generals and others were marquises.
He ranked himself among the noble,
holding the Śākya clan in profound reverence and savoring the sounds of the Dharma;
he relinquished his former residence to establish the Benqi Monastery.
Cai Ge, a former Commandant of the Zhou Yizhou Prefecture and newly appointed Governor of Xinzhou, was a court attendant at the Golden Horse Gate.
He debated Confucian learning in the Shiqu Hall and composed fu-poems in Liang Garden.
He encountered equals of Zou and Mei;
he followed the Liang dynasty into the Zhou.
His ritual propriety surpassed that of Shen and Bai.

Wang Jing, General of Wide Reach (Weiyuan Jiangjun) of the Zhou Prefectural Commandant, made offerings to Wuhansi. The Zhou Grand General Heji Xiong built Hejisi. The Zhou Grand General Ermian Yong built Ermiansi. The Zhou Director of the Mint (Sijin Dafu) Poduolaji built Pudulosi. Honghegong Yiliqin Zhongqing, the Zhou Military Commandant (Jun Sima), built Yiliqinsi. The above are from the Zhou dynasty.

During the Sui dynasty, the Emperor’s Crown Prince Yang Yong continuously commissioned the creation of statues and the transcription of scriptures; the recitation and practice of the Way proceeded without interruption at that time. In the capital, Prince Qin Wang Jun of the Sui built Yanxing Temple, a convent for the salvation of nuns; in Jingzhou, he built Kaihua Temple. In Yizhou, Prince Shu Wang Xiu of the Sui built Konghui Temple, Faju Temple, Dajianchang Temple, and Gongyang Xiaojing Temple.

Lady Changsun, Consort of Prince Xiu of Shu during the Sui dynasty, established Zhaofeng Temple. Yuan Yan, the Governor of Yizhou and Marquis of Changping during the Sui dynasty, established Zaofeng Temple. Prince Liang of Han during the Sui dynasty established Chanding Temple in the capital.
In Bingzhou, they constructed Neihua Temple and Farin Temple,
each ordaining one hundred monks and providing for their sustenance.
These were the three kings mentioned above.
Both held reverent faith within their hearts and intended to circulate [this teaching].
Among them, King Qin was most preeminent in his sincere affection, benevolence, and filial piety;
he constantly observed the six fast days and regularly practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
The scripture records his devotion to the sites where he commissioned images.
During his tenure as the Governor of Xiangzhou,
he pacified and transformed the people through his guidance, winning their hearts to a great degree.
Popular verses celebrated the arrival of the "Coming of the Savior," and it was said that even at night,
the halls and pavilions of Yanxing and Jidu were entirely occupied by the King as his own quarters.
He donated it to establish a monastery.
Li Mu, the Grand Master, Senior Pillar of State, and Duke of Shenguo of the Sui dynasty, constructed Xianshan Monastery; his character was noble and eminent, and his demeanor was pure and expansive.
With extraordinary merit and magnificent achievements,
he brought universal relief to the living people; yet when the Way of Zhou declined,
the three frontiers boiled over like a cauldron.
In the region of Suning, he suppressed the wicked and depraved;
his refined sincerity and loyal devotion penetrated both the realms of the unseen and the seen.
His resolve was profound and far-reaching, and his reputation extended to distant lands.
His meritorious achievements were established early on,
and his noble rank was exalted at an early age;
with profound virtue and the ultimate Way, he sat as a stabilizing force for refined customs.
At that time, Zong Renjie, a distinguished figure of the court and a pillar of state decorum,
employed cypress from Mount Culei and cedar from Mount Xinfu.
He constructed the Buddha hall and erected monastic quarters;
from the meditation chambers to the bell towers, all were exquisitely beautiful.
The lecture halls and gatehouses were likewise lofty and magnificent.
The late Sui Grand Protector, Upper Pillar of State, Duke of Xue, Changsun Lan, founded Jishi Temple on Lingling Mountain.
Its harmony and purity were such that the mountain courtyard and its curved eaves mysteriously corresponded to the virtue of the "Assisting Banner."
With markings like a tortoise shell and eyes like those of a river-horse, he possessed a celestial and world-transcending bearing;
his filial piety served as a model for all.
Loyalty served as his guiding principle;
he possessed a nature of gentleness, reverence, broadmindedness, and magnanimity,
as well as a talent for simplicity, refinement, and far-reaching greatness.
His way of governing the state and prospering the family,
and his strategy for rectifying the world and saving the age,
possessed the resolute spirit of Zhou She.
With solemn reverence, I cherish the spirit of Guan Zhong;
even the "Ten Chaos-Quellers" could not surpass him,
nor could the "Three Sages" compare to him.
This is what is meant by the saying, "How excellent are these pillars and limbs!
Nevertheless, he turned his merit toward the Dharma-source and revered the Śākya school.
He relinquished his ancestral residence and exhausted his halls and buildings to provide for the sacred ground, immediately constructing a jeweled monastery.
The moon-palace, golden figures, lotus pedestals,
and jeweled canopies are all exquisitely adorned and radiantly new in every detail.

Created by Yang Xiong, the Prince of Shou, who held the rank of Grand Marshal of the State (Shangzhuguo) and was the Governor-General of Huainan and Prefect of Shouzhou during the Sui Dynasty, this temple is established as a refuge for those with the talent to subdue violence and quell disturbances.
The strategies for repelling insults and managing state affairs have been fully realized;
the utility of his "claws and fangs" having been made manifest,
the power of his "eagle-soaring" prowess has accordingly been proclaimed.
He brings glory to his country and his family; his influence may be great and enduring.
As a pillar of state, he is a model for all, and as a man of letters, he is looked up to by all.
He places supreme faith in the words of the Dharma, tirelessly drawing others toward it.
He founded Xingfu Temple and constantly established offerings as a donor;
his descendants have held the rank of prince and marquis, and their lineage has transmitted the office of Grand Preceptor.
He realized emptiness while discerning existence.
Having served the Way and known its ultimate refuge, his reputation grew ever higher while his mind became ever more humble.
Dou Yi, the Grand Marshal of the Sui Dynasty, the Pillar-of-State and Duke Shenwu Su, founded Yunhua Temple; from his youth, he was celebrated for his excellent reputation.
His fame reached far among men of talent;
his household possessed imperial books bestowed upon him,
and his gate was marked by ceremonial halberds.
Throughout his service to four emperors, he maintained a single-minded devotion from beginning to end.
His sense of righteousness was as profound as dragon-patterned silk;
his regard for wealth was as slight as a cicada’s wing.
In adjudicating legal cases, he was moved by thoughts of compassion;
in governing his subordinates, he fully embodied the benevolence of broad tolerance and harmony.
Furthermore, he protected and sustained the Triple Gem while thoroughly understanding the five families of practitioners.
He made the construction of monasteries and the hosting of vegetarian feasts his constant occupation.

Those who committed theft will take birth as pigs or sheep, slaughtering their own flesh to repay their debts to others. Those who were licentious will become pigeons or fierce serpents.
Those who engaged in double-tongued speech will become owls, screech-owls, or crows.
When people hear their evil reputation, they all curse them to death.
Those who have incurred debts become donkeys, mules, horses, oxen, fish, turtles, and the like.
Beneath a large house, there is an earth-dwelling (*bhūmivivara*); one door faces north and another faces south.
Those who were called out entered through the northern gate and exited through the southern gate;
they all transformed their bodies into birds and beasts.
Furthermore, he saw a city one hundred li in length and breadth.
Among them, those who dwell peacefully during the rains retreat find joy;
when thoughts arise, they do not commit unwholesome deeds,
nor do they see the heavenly realms, yet they do not undergo suffering.
It was called the City of Ghosts.
After a year, he emerged as a human being.
He then saw another city, more than five thousand paces in width.
It is called hell.
Those who are punished therein cannot endure the agony;
they return to seek their families for one lifetime to have the punishment expiated.
All of them are within this city.
There are five or six hundred thousand men and women,
all of whom are naked and without clothing.
Emaciated by hunger and exhaustion, they supported one another.
Upon seeing Tai, they prostrated themselves and wept.
Tai asked the officials:
"How many *li* apart are the gates of the heavenly realm and the hell realm?
He replied, "The gates of the heavenly realm and the hell realm face one another; I walked around them in a complete circuit and returned.
The presiding official asked:
"Is the administration of hell according to the Dharma?
Since you have no offenses, I have appointed you as the Commander-in-Chief of the Water Office.
Otherwise, you would be no different from those within hell."
Tài asked, "When a person dies, what is it that constitutes happiness?
The master replied,
"Only for a disciple of the Buddha who is diligent and does not violate the prohibitive precepts is there happiness."
Furthermore, when one has not yet served the Buddha, transgressions pile up like mountains.
Now that one serves the Dharma, can those transgressions be eliminated?
He replied, "They are all eliminated."
The Lord summoned the Messenger of the Capital Records and asked,
"For what reason has Zhao Wenhé come to die?
The messenger opened the sealed scroll and examined the registers of his years.
There remain thirty years of his allotted lifespan,
yet he has been seized by malevolent spirits;
I now dispatch him back to his home.
For this reason, both the great and the small have resolved their minds to serve the Buddha, performing merit-making assemblies by hanging banners and canopies for their grandparents and siblings.
Wang Tan harbored doubts, yet the death of Qie served as verification; this is recorded in the *Xu Soushen Ji* (Continued Records of the Search for the Divine).
The śramaṇa Zhu Fadu was formerly a close friend of Wang Tanzhi, the General of the Household of the Central Command.
They frequently engaged in discussions together concerning the matters of birth and death, as well as the retribution of sins and blessings.
Vague and obscure, difficult to clarify, and uncertain as to whether it exists or not,
they nevertheless made this a fundamental tenet:
that although the body is first impermanent, its spirit possesses consciousness.
Regarding the determination of transgressions and merits,
one should respond with their respective signs.
Later, while Wang Tan was in the capital, he suddenly saw the Master arrive.
The king was startled and asked,
"Venerable sir, from where have you come?
He replied:
This humble monk shall pass away on such-and-such a day and month.
Both sin and merit are never in vain;
they follow one like a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound.
"Dan-yue, you need only diligently cultivate the Way and its virtue to elevate and deliver your spirit.
I have come to speak with you because of our prior agreement.
Having finished speaking, he vanished. Before the five-tiered stupa was completed, Gao Gou of Yingyang, who was already fifty years old, was executed by the blade.
Having been imprisoned in the dungeon with his neck bound in chains for the crime of murder,
he was certain that his end was near.
A fellow prisoner said to him:
Strive together to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.
If you say, "My transgressions are so grave that I am willing to accept death," [then do so].
"How can this be avoided?
he asked, urging them to observe the prohibitions together;
thus, they first gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
"I vow to abandon evil and practice good;
I shall single-mindedly call upon Avalokiteśvara without distinction between moments of leisure or urgency.
If I am thus able to escape and be delivered,"
He vowed to erect a five-storied stupa and offered himself as a slave to serve the Sangha;
within ten days, through his focused application of mind, his shackles fell away of their own accord.
The Surveillance Commissioner was struck with amazement and said to Gao Gou, "The Buddha and the gods have taken pity on you; even if you are executed, you shall not die.
On the day he was to be executed, the executioner raised his blade but did not strike.
The blade broke and the edge snapped, whereby he was granted a pardon upon petition;

this is recorded in the *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Verified Accounts) and the *Xu sushen ji* (Continued Records of the Search for the Divine). Furthermore, a goose was about to be slaughtered when it dreamed that its form was restored whole; this occurred during the reign of Wang Xi (Wang Xi of Langya), the Governor of Wuxing in the Song dynasty.
There was a scholar who cherished the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi but did not believe in the Buddha;
he devoted himself solely to the slaughter of animals.
Initially, he served as a Langzhong (Minister of the Secretariat) in the Western Province of Jin.
He was very fond of hosting guests.
In his private quarters, he kept a pair of geese that he raised;
he cherished them and took great delight in playing with them.
Believing he had attained the true nature,
he suddenly dreamed one night that a goose came with a scroll of scripture held in its beak.
It was about ten sheets of paper;
upon taking it up and looking at it, he saw that they all spoke of matters concerning sin and merit.
Indeed, when morning came, he saw that it was actually a Buddhist scripture.
Consequently, he refrained from killing.

His sincere faith surpassed that of others, and later his wealth and status increased. Guo Quan manifested himself to promote the assembly of the Dharma; Guo Quan, the Regional Inspector of Yizhou, subsequently passed away.
More than twenty years had passed.

Only then can one avoid [calamity].
Suddenly, he was no longer seen.

This is recorded in the *Xuanyan ji* (Record of Manifested Verifications): Yu Wen, sailing across the sea, did not fear the great waves. Yu Wen was transporting salt in the South Sea when he encountered a wind.

at the time, this was considered a divine miracle.

This account appears in the *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Manifested Miracles). During the eighth year of the Yuanjia era, a great fire broke out in the city of Puyuan in Hedong that could not be extinguished, yet the vihāra did not burn.
Only the monasteries, large and small, remained solemnly intact;

The common people were struck with wonder and redoubled their resolve to cultivate the mind.

From the *Chu xian ji* (Records of Manifested Verifications): A Goose Dies and Then Cries Again at the Tianmiao Temple in Jiankang. In the main street of Jiankang Commandery, there was a temple to the Four Heavenly Kings.

Upon examining the back of the statue's neck,
he found three knife scars; seeing this,

The *Chu xian ji* (Records of Manifested Verifications) relates that when the temple deity offered him silk, he was immediately freed from his python body. "As for the śramaṇa An Shigao..."
He was the crown prince of the King of Parthia.
The *An-shih-chieh ching* (Ānāpāna-smṛti-sūtra) was a work produced by him.
He once traveled to Yuzhang and reached Gongting Lake.
The temple deity said to An Shigao:
"In the past, I lived in a foreign land where I left the household life to become a practitioner of the Way.
I delighted in practicing generosity but did not observe the precepts."
Today, I serve as the deity of Gongting Lake here;
for a circumference of one thousand li, all is under my jurisdiction.
The common people present me with countless precious offerings and curiosities.
"This is the retribution for the harm I inflicted upon myself in my previous life.
Had I been able to maintain the precepts, the merit would have led to rebirth in heaven;
because I violated the prohibitions, I have fallen into this state as a spirit. You were my fellow student; it is now that we meet."
My grief and joy are beyond words;
my life will end in days or nights,
yet this hideous form grows ever larger.
"I do not wish to cast off my life here and defile the lake waters;
I shall instead cross over to the empty marsh beyond the western mountain.
I fear that after this body perishes, I may fall into hell."
"I have one thousand bolts of silk and various miscellaneous items within a stone casket;
you may use these to erect a stupa and support the Three Jewels."
"May I, after passing from this life, be reborn in a favorable realm.
Entrusting himself deeply to him with these words,
An Shigao wept with tears streaming down his face.
He then said to the spirit,
"Why do you not manifest your form so that we may speak face to face?
The spirit replied:
"The form of one who has violated the precepts is exceedingly ugly;
seeing it would surely cause alarm and fear. Lokakṣema said:
"I am not afraid even if you briefly manifest your form.
Then a spirit emerged from behind the bed with its head; it was a great python.
It went to the side of An Shigao’s knees, and its tears fell like rain.
He did not know where the tail’s length or location was;
suddenly it entered behind the bed.
Thereupon, An Shigao collected the silk items.
Having placed everything inside the boat, they took their leave and departed.
The companions set their sails all at once and proceeded on their way.
The deity again assumed the form of a serpent, ascended to the mountain peak, gazed after them from afar, and then vanished.
The flames were extinguished only after the multitude raised their hands.
In an instant, he reached Yuzhang,
where he immediately founded Dongsi Temple within that region.
The deity immediately moved it;

The present-day She Village in Xunyang Commandery is that very place.
After An Shigao returned to the capital, he used the remaining items from the temple to erect a three-story pagoda at Waguan Temple.
Later, An Shigao dreamed that a deity came to inform him:

This is also recorded in the *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Manifested Miracles). As for the mother of Che, she lit a lamp and did not expect her son to arrive; the mother of Che suffered the disaster of the "Green Mud" at the hands of the Prince of Luling during the Song dynasty and was captured by the Northern Xiongnu. While he was in the midst of the enemy camp,

Day and night, she concentrated her mind on weeping for Avalokiteśvara,

She continued in this manner for a year.
His son suddenly managed to escape and return;

The Record of Manifested Verifications was published by Kong Qiong of the Ministry of Personnel.

The retribution for sins and merits is fixed and unfailing.

This is from the *Chujiong biezhuan*.

As for the Daoist Shi Jun, he was able to walk after bathing a statue; Shi Jun was one whose learning and knowledge were devoted to the Dao while he held the Buddha in contempt, often saying to others:
