It is possible to prolong one's life and obtain blessings; few fail to attain longevity by reverently upholding the Dharma.

This is recorded in the *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Manifested Verifications). Liu Shi, a Minister of the Interior, deeply contemplated the image and returned it to Pengcheng. This is from the biography of Liu Shi.
He constantly made offerings to a single image,
which he lost for no apparent reason and could not find its whereabouts.
Shi then contemplated his transgressions day and night, reproaching himself.
Through his profound mindfulness, there was a mysterious communion;
after one hundred days had passed,
the image suddenly appeared of its own accord upon its original seat.
A divine light illuminated the chamber;
the entire family was struck with wonder and joy,
and their devotion redoubled.
The *Chuxian ji* (Records of Manifested Verifications) states that Liu Yimin was a man of refined thought and diligent devotion.
His pearl-like countenance shone with radiance between his eyebrows. Liu Yimin was a native of Pengcheng;
in his youth he was a Confucian scholar, and his filial piety toward his deceased parents became renowned.
His family was poor, so he divined a site for a dwelling in the forest west of Mount Xi.
Suffering from many ailments, he did not set his heart on wife or children;
he cut off all social visits and devoted himself to the diligent cultivation of meditation.
Within half a year, he beheld the mark between the eyebrows;
gradually, he saw one eye of the Buddha,
as well as the two colors at the hairline.
Furthermore, he saw his entire body,
which he took to be a painted image;
he also saw a Daoist practitioner offering him a bright pearl.
Consequently, his illness was cured.
This is recorded in the *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Manifested Miracles). During the reign of Sun Hao, King Wu surrounded the monastery and seized the monks;
at that time, the śarīra emitted a radiant light above the alms bowl. Wang Zhengbian submitted a memorial regarding this matter.
"The Buddha-dharma should be extinguished in the Middle Kingdom; it is not beneficial for the spirits of the barbarians.
Consequently, Sun Hao issued an edict to assemble all the śramaṇas, arrayed his troops, surrounded the monasteries, and intended to carry out their execution and the abolition of the religion.
He said to the assembly of monks and the Dharma Master,
"If the Buddha is indeed a deity,
we ought to venerate him."
If there were no spirit,
the one in black robes would share the same fate as the others in a single day;
perhaps the monk would even hang himself to death.
Some fled outside.
Hui then purified himself for a seven-day period and manifested a divine transformation:
he placed a copper bowl filled with water in the courtyard.
After the midday meal was finished, the sunlight shone brilliantly.

and then suddenly the śarīra appeared.
A brilliant light illuminated the courtyard and hovered above the alms bowl.
Fahu and the great assembly watched from before it, struck with such awe and alarm that they were at a loss for what to do.
Nanxi changed his expression and stepped forward.
Huì said: "If Your Majesty were to employ the strength of Mengben to strike with a mallet weighing a hundred *jīn*,
the adamantine nature [of this object] would ultimately not be destroyed."
Senghao followed these instructions.
He first requested that the monks perform the chanting of scriptures, prostrations, and the scattering of flowers while burning incense.
With a loud voice, he proclaimed his sincere devotion, invoking Maitreya until the ferry to the Pure Land was no longer interrupted.
Then the Wheel of Dharma will be turned,
penetrating the path of the numinous;
its majestic spiritual power shall be no small matter.
"You should manifest yourself this very day;
otherwise, the Three Jewels will be extinguished forever.
Having spoken these words, the warrior struck his fist with a sound like a gale.
Those who witnessed it were struck with trembling and their breath was exhausted.
When they smashed the śarīra, it remained undamaged;
a brilliant light emerged, its radiant colors filling the pillars.
Emperor Huai submitted himself in sincere devotion and diligently organized vegetarian feasts and lectures.
This stupa was located north of the Great Market in Jiankang;
even later, it continued to manifest auspicious radiance.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year of the Yuanjia era, the temple spire emitted a brilliant light at night;
a vivid crimson radiance burst forth,
and a flame-like glow circled from the west toward the south above the fourth story.
Furthermore, he saw an object resembling a pheasant-tail fan;
its name was not clearly known as it moved with his advancing and halting.
Those who observed him sometimes encountered it and sometimes did not.
For about twenty days, everyone in the capital city saw a great purple light atop the stupa.
This is recorded in the *Wulu* and the *Xuanyan ji*. Regarding Dingling’s savage rebellion and his shooting at the [Buddha’s] moon-like face until he was executed, the *Xuanyan ji* states:
In the city of Ye in Xiangzhou, there was a sixteen-foot standing image made of pure gold.
It encountered the Chanyu of the Dingling,
who was by nature extremely fierce and violent.
Lacking faith, he drew his bow and shot at the image;
the arrow struck the face of the image, and blood flowed down in rivulets.
Although it was polished and adorned, the bloodstains still remained.
Furthermore, five hundred strong men were selected to pull it down to the ground.
As they were about to smelt it down into copper for the purpose of making ritual vessels, the image suddenly uttered a loud voice, its resonance like a crashing thunderclap.
The strength of the laborers was extinguished and their souls lost their courage; everyone fell to the ground, overwhelmed by confusion and rolling about in distress.
Terrified, they were unable to rise;
because of this, the bandits’ hearts were momentarily struck with alarm, and the number of those who returned to the faith increased.
Later, the Dīnglíng fell ill and was executed and died; Hélián was likewise cruel and obstinate.
Regarding the account of dying while wearing monastic robes during the earthquake, the *Xuanyan ji* states:
When the Fuqu barbarians destroyed the territory of Jizhou, both monastics and laypeople were utterly slaughtered; their cruelty and violent chaos left no one unslain.
By the time it reached Guanzhong, more than half of the population had perished;
the corpses of women and children were piled up until they formed mountains,
yet those who harbored such malice took pleasure in their cruelty.
He further said to himself:
"The Buddhas are the Buddhas among men;
they are worthy of receiving prostrations."
He then had an image of the Buddha painted;
wearing it upon his back, he sat within the hall and commanded the śramaṇas of the realm to bow toward his back to pay homage to the image.
He immediately prostrated himself before me.
Later, while we were out on a journey,
a violent storm suddenly broke out, and the four directions became dark and obstructed.
Not knowing where he had gone,
[the king] was struck dead by a thunderclap amidst the roar of lightning and thunder.
After his burial, [the king] appeared at the site of the thunderclap.
His coffin was burned and his corpse exposed outside; his back was inscribed with characters such as "tyrannical and unprincipled.
The people of the country rejoiced, lamenting that he had died too late.

Xiao Zixian of the Qi Shu records that when Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty extensively destroyed monasteries, the pus flowed from his entire body.
Having severely devastated the Triple Gem and demolished temples and stupas,

The ministers deliberated on the matter, concluding that it was the work of the Buddha’s divine power; this is recorded in the biography of Cui Hao. When Yuwen [Xuan] abolished the monastic order, his entire body broke out in festering sores.
Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, having destroyed and abolished the Three Honored Ones, subsequently developed a malignant ulcer at the Wangyi Palace.
After ten days had passed without improvement, he suddenly passed away. Xie Hai destroyed the stupa, and [the monk] suffered from chronic illness for many years. The *Jin Lu* states:
"Before the Minister Xie Hai had yet resolved his mind [for the Dharma]..."
He served as the Regional Inspector of Jingzhou and declared that Buddhist temples and stupas were inappropriate for the human world;
he intended to relocate them outside the city walls.

eighty soldiers, each holding a sword and an axe,

Furthermore, he saw two figures, both over ten feet tall,
with magnificent and imposing statures, staring with eyes full of wrath and speaking in a stern voice:
"The conduct you have pursued deviates from the Way."
Soon you shall see for yourself.
Subsequently, the officials and attendants of that party all contracted leprosy and died after some time;
the others were all executed for their crimes.
Xie Hai suffered from chronic emaciation and illness for many years;

later, due to his involvement in a rebellion, his entire family was executed, and he died an unnatural death. According to the *Xuanyan ji*, Sun Hao once indulged himself in sexual excesses, resulting in painful inflammation of the genitals that persisted for months.
The ruler of Wu, Sun Hao, was by nature extremely violent and cruel.
His actions were devoid of human feeling;
once, he went with his court ladies to supervise the cultivation of the garden soil.
Suddenly, he obtained a golden image;
its features were brilliant and majestic.
Emperor Hao ordered that the image be placed beside the latrine.
The messenger held a tally behind his back;
on the eighth day of the fourth month,
Senghao then immersed it above the head of the statue.
He laughed and said,
"Today is the eighth day; I shall confer the empowerment upon you as a source of amusement amidst these court ladies."
After some time had passed, his scrotum suddenly became swollen;
the pain and high fever were unbearable.
From night until dawn, he suffered in agony, seeking death.
The eminent physicians treated him with the finest medicines, yet his condition only grew worse.
The Grand Astrologer divined that this was caused by the transgression of a Great Deity and issued an edict ordering prayers at the spirit temples.
With every prayer, his illness intensified; there was no remedy for those above or below.
In the inner palace there was a lady-in-waiting who had previously followed the Buddha-dharma and possessed internal knowledge.
Whatever he recorded was often remarkably accurate.
He reported, saying:
"Your Majesty has not yet sought the Buddha-image."
Seng Hao asked,
"Is the Buddha a great deity?
The girl replied:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, none is more venerable than the Buddha.
The image Your Majesty previously obtained still remains beside the latrine;
please retrieve it and offer worship."
The swelling was surely cured immediately.
Emperor Hao, distressed by the urgency of his pain, promptly prepared fragrant water and washed the image with his own hands, then placed it upon the dais in the hall.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground to apologize for his transgression and single-mindedly sought compassion.
